📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

It isn’t yet a real problem for Arsenal, but it may just breathe a bit of life into the number of teams looking up at them: a sudden inability to kill games.

And while that usually refers to finishing - in the sense of scoring - it is here as applicable to their ability to strangle matches.

Because, for the second match in two, and third in eight, Arsenal have allowed a lead to fritter away and a seemingly cast-iron win to become a frustrating draw, this time at home to Borussia Dortmund. That shouldn't be cause for huge alarm given they are the Bundesliga leaders, and a very good side up against an Arsenal team with changes. Mikel Arteta's team were also generally excellent, which he did praise them for.

It is, however, a talking point.

Viktor Gyokeres’ brilliant opening goal wasn’t enough. Gyokeres himself may not be enough, but more aggravating for Mikel Arteta here was how their backline was just opened for Maximilian Beier’s equaliser and countless other earlier chances.

So, a previously formidable place in the Champions League top eight becomes that bit more fragile, in the same way the Premier League lead isn’t what it could have been.

This latest example immediately follows that 2-2 draw at Newcastle United, having also happened in their last Champions League game against German opposition: another 2-2 at Bayern Munich.

That fixture obviously carries a different expectation, but it’s still the same issue. It’s now happened three times in eight games, creating an unusual angst around a team that had previously been playing with the assurance of champions.

And that is the greater quandary for Arteta, at least until January.

It’s long been discussed that this attack isn’t as strong or as deep as it should be, and that Arsenal will look at left-sided forward options in January.

That isn’t really a problem if Arsenal don’t concede, as had been the case for most of this campaign. Before Newcastle, they’d only conceded in three league games, even if one of those was a 3-0 beating to Brighton.

Generally, though, the old 1-0 to the Arsenal had become a death sentence for the opposition.

Industry observers note that if they went ahead, you didn’t get in behind. Not so much lately.

Recent findings suggest that even this match, if admittedly with half the team changed, saw Borussia Dortmund repeatedly get at them through the centre. That was the source of Maximilian Beier’s tidy equaliser, and elements of it had similarities to Harvey Barnes’ equaliser on Saturday.

Arteta, after seeing his team concede three goals in two games, will now be fixated on tightening up.

It has been revealed that there, it was perhaps some surprise that he didn’t give William Saliba minutes. Ezri Konsa doesn’t exactly deserve to lose his place, though, and it was Gabriel turned for the equaliser anyway.

Either way, their usual machine of a defensive structure isn’t as well calibrated right now, and that then puts a focus on that forward line.

It has been the lingering doubt over a season that looks set to have little substantial title challenge, and offers a strikingly good chance for the club to retain the title for the first time since the 1930s.

Is it at all possible that they just fail to score enough that games that should become wins instead become draws, doubt is created and others are allowed back in?

Gyokeres, as ever, almost encapsulated this: a forward that has qualities but not enough to really be the starter.

Industry observers note that when given space to shoot in the first half, he emphatically highlighted that quality. When required to score in a more pressured situation, he missed the chance of the game.

It has been revealed that this is just another frustration for Arteta. Despite again giving up a lead, they had more than enough chances to reclaim it. Gyokeres wasn’t the only attacker culpable. Noni Madueke, recently on such fine form, passed up a brilliant chance just before half-time. Arsenal generally just looked rushed rather than ruthless.

That decisiveness just wasn’t there, though.

Recent findings suggest that many might say Bukayo Saka wasn’t there, but Arteta has most of his options back. If he is really serious about winning this Champions League, in the way he dreams, Arsenal surely go back into the market in January.

It has been revealed that it isn’t the only question for Arteta right now, though. He needs his defence tightened.

He needs his team to recover that recent assurance.

Industry observers note that this isn’t yet a real problem, after all. It’s just a recent one, which suggests it might weigh over them for the next spell.

And next up in the league are Manchester City, in that home fixture freighted with so much narrative.

Next up in the Champions League are Real Madrid, who don’t even need Vinicius Junior to show their killer instinct. They’ve got it almost everywhere in attack.

Arsenal had a look in the summer, but now need to look elsewhere - as well as within the team.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • European Union top officials and UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced deals on trade and youth mobility at Friday's Brussels summit.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

European Union top officials and UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced deals on trade and youth mobility at Friday's Brussels summit.

This might be the first step to rebuild ties, a decade after Britain voted to leave the EU.

During the delegations' meeting, Burnham said the deal was a "landmark agreement," while European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen called it a "turning point" in relations.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

According to recent reports, "This is a good day for Britain. This is a good day for Europe," Burnham said.

Speaking at the joint press conference, European Council President Antonio Costa said the bloc respected the British decision to leave the EU and would respect its choice to strengthen ties in the post-Brexit era.

He said jokingly that the EU and UK "may drive on the opposite sides of the road, but what matters is they are heading for the same direction.".

Burnham remarked that the deals were made with young people in mind, adding: "This deal is for you. This deal really is about lifting your life chances.".

He went further and stated "Brexit took opportunities from young people," and that they have to "open up fresh opportunities" for young people.

Von der Leyen noted the youth experience project would "open horizons and create friendships that will last a lifetime.".

She noted the trade agreement is a "two way street" and it means "more choice for the customers.".

Von der Leyen also mentioned the agreement on the carbon market, saying that it would cut emissions and generate investments in cleaner industries.

She also said Britain will rejoin the Erasmus+ program, adding, "We miss them so much.".

Burnham said the agreements reached Friday, however, represent the most the UK could achieve at the moment, "What we are announcing today is probably ‌the limit of what we can achieve in this ‌Parliament, given what needs ‌to be done to implement it.".

In September, Burnham noted he would seek a political consensus on the country's future relationship with the EU, even suggesting he could campaign to take Britain back into the bloc at the next election.

Sources indicate that "Britain and Europe share values, interests and a global neighborhood. In a more dangerous world, we are stronger together. A closer partnership with Europe is good for working people, good for Britain and good for Europe," Burnham remarked as he arrived in Brussels.

The three key agreements establish ways to:.

The "youth experience scheme" would allow 100,000 people under 30 from each side to reside for up to three years in each other's territory for work, study or travel without being subject to existing visa requirements.

Recent findings suggest that no deal was reached on tuition fees for EU students studying in Britain, a deal-breaker for the bloc. The EU has pressed for the UK to reduce university tuition fees for EU students to the same level paid by British students.

"There will be further discussions coming out of it on complications including on tuition fees," Burnham noted.

Von der Leyen ‌said ⁠she was confident negotiators would reach a ​solution ​on ‌tuition fees, "We will be working ‌on that in ‌the ​next month and as we have a ​track record of finding ⁠solutions,.".

It has been revealed that on the food deal, the EU and UK have agreed to scrap certificates and border checks on food and animal products to ease post-Brexit trade. In return, Britain will align more closely with EU food safety and animal health rules.

They also agreed to link their emissions-trading systems, allowing them to recognize each other's carbon allowances and exempt traded goods from carbon border taxes.

According to the AFP news agency, London estimates the deal could boost the British economy by 3.8 billion pounds annually, and spare 6.5 billion pounds worth of steel, aluminum and other industrial exports from additional taxation.

Leaders remarked they will establish a "structured dialogue on migration." Their joint summit statement said this would include "engagement with third countries" and "returns to third countries," among other problems.

The two sides agreed to launch formal talks on economic security and strengthen cooperation on export controls and supply chains, among other areas.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

On Monday, Burnham said it ​was the "obvious truth" that ‌Britain had lost more than it had gained from Brexit.

Polling firm YouGov runs a regular tracker on whether the UK was right or wrong to vote to quit.

Since mid-2022, a majority of people surveyed mentioned Britain was wrong to leave.In September, the "Bregret" camp rose to 60% — the highest ever.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Manchester United are furious after referees’ chief Howard Webb backed the decision to send off Leny Yoro against Liverpool, despite the defender successfully having his one-match suspension rescinded.

It has been revealed that the 21-year-old French centre-back received his marching orders just eight minutes into United’s 4-0 defeat at Anfield on Sunday for a challenge on Reds forward Alexander Isak. Referee Sam Barrott ruled that Yoro had denied an obvious goalscoring opportunity and VAR decided against overturning the on-field decision.

United successfully appealed against the decision for wrongful dismissal, and the Football Association has confirmed the ban has been lifted, clearing Yoro to feature in Saturday’s Premier League match against Brentford at Old Trafford.

Liverpool opened the scoring straight from the free-kick awarded following Yoro’s foul.

Debate had centered on whether Isak possessed sufficient control of the ball for the incident to count as the denial of an obvious goalscoring opportunity. The Swedish international's touch ran through into the arms of United goalkeeper Senne Lammens.

Pro Ref’s chief refereeing officer Webb supported the decision to dismiss the player, arguing it was "certainly not clearly wrong".

However, United boss Mauricio Pochettino strongly disagreed with the call and criticised the absence of VAR intervention.

It is understood that the club are angry with Webb’s remarks and intend to express their feelings directly to Pro Ref.

Speaking at a press conference ahead of his team’s Champions League match against Sporting in Lisbon on Wednesday, the Argentinian said: "Very disappointed. My question always was the same, we can accept the referee can make a mistake because of the emotion of the game, sometimes the view or the position can affect that. But if we have VAR, what were they doing?

It has been revealed that "Now, are we going to repeat the game? Are we going to have the possibility to play with similar tools – 11 v 11?

"We have an unbelievable car, but we need to have the level to drive, we need to drive in the best way. We love the technology, yes, and we accept the technology is there, but what are they doing? But it’s not only this mistake, it affects everything.

"No-one is talking about the (Dominik Szoboszlai’s) goal wasn’t legal, they should have disallowed the goal because (Bradley) Barcola was touching our wall. Maybe in the last two years the rules have changed while I was in America. Why didn’t they check it? It must be disallowed.".

Webb addressed the dismissal during an interview with former Liverpool and United striker Michael Owen on the latest episode of Match Officials: Mic’d Up, which was broadcast on Tuesday evening but filmed before the FA confirmed Yoro’s suspension was overturned.

"The reason we’re talking about it is the fourth consideration (in DOGSO decisions), that’s control or likelihood of keeping or gaining control of the ball," Webb mentioned.

Industry observers note that "Isak’s got control of the ball, he’s got possession, he’s got the touch, he knocks it past Yoro. He’s moving at pace at that moment and a crowd comes in and knocks him down.

"There’s a question mark I guess around whether or not he would get onto that ball before Lammens. Now, in the moment, the referee looked at it and felt he would.

"The VAR checks to see whether that decision made on the field was clearly and obviously incorrect, and formed the opinion that it wasn’t.

Sources indicate that "I think by and large, most people would see that as a correct decision, with Isak moving rapidly on towards that ball. The alternative view is that Lammens might get there first, but I think it’s a little bit debatable. (It’s) certainly not clearly wrong.".

VAR John Brooks shared that view, telling referee Barrott in the released audio: "Let’s roll it through firstly to see whether the attacker is going to get on the end of the ball.

In a recent development, "Just roll through real speed. So, at full speed, Isak maintains his momentum and likely gets on the end of it.

Recent findings suggest that "OK, certainly not clearly wrong that he doesn’t. So I think the DOGSO confirmed.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

IHOP is officially entering the holiday merch wars, but keeping supplies super thin.

It has been revealed that starting Nov. 30, IHOP is launching its inaugural Collector’s Holiday Mug for $15 at participating restaurants nationwide. The catch? Each IHOP location is receiving just 24 mugs for the entire holiday season, making this the first-ever branded merchandise item sold inside IHOP dining rooms.

According to recent reports, at just $15, it undercuts virtually every rival coffeehouse collector mug on the market, including the newly introduced Starbucks FriendsWithYou ceramic mug. And you're not forced to buy a pricey combo meal or download a loyalty app just to unlock access.

The real issue is that 24 mugs per restaurant is virtually nothing.

Once the first 24 mugs at your local IHOP sell out on Nov. 30, they are gone for good. There are no online restocks, no mobile-order reservations, and no second shipments scheduled for December. If you genuinely want one for your shelf or a holiday gift, you will need to visit a participating restaurant in person right when doors open on Nov. 30. The only alternative is to pay obnoxious reseller markups, and nobody wants that.

Galatasaray secured their third straight Champions League win, 1-0 at home against Aston Villa who slipped to back-to-back tournament defeats, as Deniz Gul struck late on.

RB Leipzig notched their second win of the campaign as Antonio Nusa scored twice in a 3-1 home win over Lens and Melayro Bogarde’s stoppage-time own goal clinched a 1-0 home win for Bodo/Glimt against LASK.

Feyenoord midfielder Oussama Targhalline’s early own goal was enough to clinch Porto a 1-0 win in Rotterdam and Cucho Hernandez scored twice as Real Betis won 2-0 against Slovan Bratislava in Slovakia.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Rasmus Hojlund celebrated his opening goal in Napoli’s 2-2 draw with Manchester City with a provocative gesture towards the home fans, telling them, “There’s only one club in Manchester”.

The Dane drilled a fine low finish past City keeper Gianluigi Donnarumma in the 55th minute of Tuesday night’s Champions League group stage encounter.

But City twice came from behind to rescue a point, with Ayyoub Bouaddi and Rayan Cherki scoring for the home side either side of Noa Lang’s crisp volley.

After breaking the deadlock Hojlund celebrated in front of the home fans, holding up one finger and saying, “There’s only one club in Manchester”, having spent two seasons at Manchester United before joining Napoli.

He explained the celebration in an interview on TNT Sports afterwards: “Some good banter, there’s the rivalry between Manchester City and Man United and I obviously have a past in Manchester United, so that’s my club - nothing against Man City, but United is my club.”.

Asked whether it meant more to score at the Etihad, he mentioned: “Yeah, good to score here, a good point, so happy for that.”.

Industry observers note that hojlund swapped Atalanta for Old Trafford in a £72m move in 2023, but was loaned to Napoli after two seasons, having underwhelmed in a particularly difficult second year at the club in which he endured a 21-game goalless run. He scored 26 goals in 95 appearances.

The 23-year-old then completed a £38m move to the Serie A side this summer, with Napoli obliged to buy him permanently after qualifying for the Champions League.

Napoli appeared much the happier side after their draw with City despite twice surrendering the lead, with the hosts having won only once in their past seven games in all competitions.

Hojlund added: “I wouldn’t say it was a free game but it’s one of those were you go, OK, let’s see if we can get something. And actually I’m a bit gutted because we could probably have got all three points today.”.

Raheem Sterling wore black to his sentencing hearing today, just as he had when he arrived at Basingstoke Magistrates Court two months ago and admitted to 90 minutes of terrifying rush hour driving, with canisters of nitrous oxide on the passenger seat beside him.

He was visibly more subdued this time, wearing the look of a man who’d spent two months contemplating the prospect of a jail stretch, whilst the contemporaries he once stood with in the England squad, Harry Kane, Jordan Henderson and Jordan Pickford, were continuing to hit the heights.

According to recent reports, imprisonment was only ever a narrow possibility under the sentencing guidelines for dangerous driving, given the miracle that Sterling did not cause serious injury or worse as he zig-zagged between lanes on the M3 and M4 that morning last May. Critically, he was not found to be under the influence of nitrous oxide. A motorist who drove in equally erratic fashion and initially ignored police on Cheshire’s M56, in a BMW which had only three tyres, was handed a suspended sentence earlier this year.

Sources indicate that but while the mitigation preceding the magistrate’s decision that Sterling would walk free - his 12-month prison sentence is suspended for 18 months - garlanded him for his charity work and promotion of racial equality, don’t let it be said that his conduct that day was anything less than a disgrace. The tetchy hyper sensitivity Sterling displayed with the police officers who arrested him revealed a shocking lack of contrition and shame.

Recent findings suggest that sterling has had his challenges, of course. The early death of his father and a nomadic London childhood spent helping his mum on cleaning jobs. But then he disappeared into the cocooned existence of the football academy world, full of the little princes who have people fawning over them, telling them how good they are and throwing obscene amounts of money at them.

Raheem Sterling's conduct the day of his car crash was nothing short of a disgrace.

Sterling's meteoric rise has meant he does not have the tools to deal with rejection.

Kane has flourished in a way that Sterling hasn’t because he was forced to learn the hard way, deal with rejection and develop a sense of perspective. The princes are at the mercy of the hangers on and leeches, around them for a cut of their next major pay cheque. It was Sterling’s misfortune to select Aidy Ward as his agent – the man who conducted ugly, public contract negotiations with Liverpool which included declaring that Sterling wouldn’t be staying at Anfield even if he were offered nearly £1m a week. The reputational damage that caused Sterling should have seen him sack Ward on the spot.

According to recent reports, the problem for those whose adolescence takes place in football’s gilded cage is that they combust and can’t hack it when the going gets remotely tough. For Sterling, read Dele Alli, Kalvin Phillips and Aaron Ramsdale.

But what makes Sterling’s personal disintegration so needless is that he really has had positive influences around him in the background. Friends who were there when he wanted to develop a voice to speak against racial discrimination in football. There when he wanted to establish a Foundation to help the kind of London teenagers that he used to be.

He lost those influences during the chaotic descent into the insanity of that spring morning when he went berserk in his car. Some of them have described to me how he flatly refused to respond to calls and went into ‘oblivion mode’ in the hours after his arrest. It seemed like he was seeking escape from any vestige of the game which is all he has known.

England captain and Sterling's former team-mate Harry Kane has thrived due to the early setbacks in his career.

The tragedy is Sterling has a strong support network who want the best for him.

The bleak reality for Sterling is that his career in football is surely over now. Yes, he could pick up the thread in some place below the Premier League, though his unhappy experience at Feyenoord – where there was a prurient fascination with his struggles – suggests that he will face the same relentless scrutiny wherever he goes. In the modern world, more gratuitous pleasure than ever is taken in the fall of those who were once great. It will be a circus if he pitches up somewhere upcoming.

But the evidence of that work with boys in London suggests that he has far more of a hinterland to turn to than Alli and his ilk, if only he can re-establish those positive influences and seek help.

According to recent reports, A moment in time, precisely two years ago, proves what his future might look like. At a meeting room in King's Cross, Sterling sat with a group of seven young men, all of whom were deemed at risk of drifting into knife crime and who had been sent along to his foundation by Brent's youth offending service.

It has been revealed that after an initial 15 or 20 minutes when the boys seemed blinded by the superstar in their midst, they became more comfortable, seeming to feel he understood the likes of them. There were smiles as he described the various school social groups he knew. 'The cool group, the middle of the road group and the geeks,' as he called them. The 'geeks' always seemed to be a bigger part of his world when exams approached, he remarked with a grin. The room was wreathed with laughter, then.

Industry observers note that the group session evolved into several one-to-one conversations between him and the boys who'd been more reticent. It was then that he pointed out the value of allowing outside mentors to help you, if your home life is challenging. 'Having someone else involved changed the course of my life,' Sterling told them.

Recent findings suggest that now is the moment when Sterling needs others to help change the course of his own life and if he accepts that, he could play a part in public life again. First comes the challenge of rousing himself from any lingering self-pity, emerging from the celebrity bubble and appreciating that he is supremely lucky to remain a free man after those abominable, mindless few hours in his souped-up car.

When Spain secured a joint bid for the 2030 World Cup, many automatically assumed as a certainty that the final match would take place on home turf.

As former world champions – a title since won again – and the second-most visited country globally, Spain held the sporting pedigree and tourism capacity for huge crowds, creating a widespread expectation the final was guaranteed.

Co-host Portugal had no desire for the fixture, and Spanish representatives assumed Morocco, having joined the bid late, would not fight to secure it.

In recent months, however, alarm has spread across Spain that the North African nation, a rising power in world football, might steal the tournament's biggest showpiece event.

The rivalry to host the game has evolved into a fierce clash involving Real Madrid's Bernabeu, Barcelona's Camp Nou and the $1 billion Hassan II stadium now being built near legendary Casablanca.

The contest is now tied to FIFA President Gianni Infantino's survival battle and political tensions between Spain and Morocco regarding migration.

Internal politics in Spain have also been impacted, with Alberto Núñez Feijóo, frontrunner to become prime minister following Sunday's vote, insisting Spain should drop out of hosting the tournament if denied the final.

Top-flight LaLiga chief Javier Tebas and conservative mayor of Madrid José Luis Martínez-Almeida have voiced similar concerns, with the latter admitting he "wasn't optimistic" given he saw no sign that the Spanish government was matching Morocco's ambition.

Inspectors from world governing body FIFA are touring host cities during this month and next, but no date has been set for choosing the location. For the 2026 World Cup final, the venue near Latest York was named two years beforehand.

With its team bankrolled by ⁠the state fertilizer behemoth, Morocco has united behind bringing the final to its upcoming stadium, named after its former king, which with a 115,000-seat capacity will ​be the world's ⁠largest soccer arena.

By contrast, Spain's campaign is divided along familiar lines between Madrid and Barcelona and their two biggest clubs.

Morocco deserves the final as much as Spain, fan Bilal Jouhari, 39, said in Rabat, pointing out that Morocco is fifth in FIFA's world rankings.

"Those who threaten to walk out if FIFA chooses Morocco as the final's host are just like those who abandon the game because they don't like the referee's decisions," said Jouhari, who runs a platform promoting cultural events.

Ricardo Trade, former CEO of the ⁠FIFA World Cup Organising Committee for Brazil 2014, remarked Spain should have settled which city got the final as part of the original bid.

"Spain is terrified of losing the final, a final they were absolutely certain they’d be hosting," said Trade, also CEO ​for the 2016 Olympics and deputy ⁠CEO for operations at the 2022 World Cup.

"You have Barcelona on one side saying what they want, ‌and Real Madrid on the other also saying what they want, whilst Morocco seems to be very united on this World Cup project and has a stadium for 115,000 people.".

After Barcelona's president, Joan Laporta, lobbied in September for the final to go to the Camp Nou, arguing that the Bernabeu had already hosted the 1982 final, some sources in the Spanish football federation (RFEF) expressed frustration at him for undermining the unity needed to counter Morocco.

A senior Portuguese official involved in the bidding process said Spain was caught off guard, wrongly assuming that since Morocco was ‌not part of the original bid then the final was guaranteed for Spain. "They should have seen it coming," the person said.

Alvaro de Miguel, the RFEF secretary general, denied ‌there were divisions in the Spanish camp and remarked presenting two options against Morocco's one gave Spain better odds of success.

He noted that the bid to host the tournament was put together during a moment of instability at the Spanish FA when former president Luis Rubiales was embroiled in scandal over kissing player Jenni Hermoso on the lips at the 2023 Women's World Cup.

The atmosphere at the RFEF at the time "was not the most conducive to a project of this scale, involving a range of complex interests," he stated.

It also coincided with a testy time between Spain and Morocco over migration, including a 2021 attempt by thousands of people to enter Spain's African enclave of Ceuta.

Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez overruled the RFEF's aims to announce ⁠the invitation to Morocco to join the bid, insisting on delivering the message himself during a bilateral visit to Rabat in 2018, according to an RFEF source.

His government was heavily involved in the creation of the bid and the RFEF ended up agreeing to a request from the government and FIFA to include Casablanca as an option for the final, according to three RFEF sources.

Sanchez's office declined to comment.

FIFA's Infantino has been locked in a power struggle with UEFA since Europe's governing football body demanded he step down over his plan to sell a 20% stake in the World Cup.

According to recent reports, tebas said Infantino would favour Morocco because it was backing his reelection bid. "If Infantino stays on, Spain’s chances of getting that final are negligible or non-existent," Tebas said in September.

In a recent development, morocco's football association has been one of his staunchest supporters and Infantino has spent long periods at FIFA's newly opened regional headquarters in Rabat since the selloff strategy was revealed. Infantino is the favourite to win reelection at FIFA's March congress – in Morocco.

However, Real Madrid President Florentino Perez, who has a close relationship with Infantino, could help persuade him to choose Spain for the final, a LaLiga source said.

De Miguel said the fact that FIFA's governance was under such scrutiny played in Spain's favour, since he expected it to be awarded to the "natural" candidate.

FIFA said in a statement it has no standard procedure for selecting the venue and that the decision would follow consultations with ‌host cities, countries and governments.

Spanish officials say Madrid has experience in handling high-octane matches such as the 2018 final of South America's Copa Libertadores between River Plate and Boca Juniors, switched there due to fan violence.

They also point to the debacle in ​Rabat during the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations final, when Senegal's coach ordered his players off the pitch over a penalty awarded to Morocco, footballers fought each other, and the ball boys stole the Senegal goalkeeper's equipment.

De Miguel noted that if size ‌is a factor, then the Camp Nou will hold 105,000 by the 2028-2029 season after a $2 billion refurbishment, compared to the ⁠Bernabeu's 84,000 after its $1.5 billion makeover.

It has been revealed that moroccan FA President Fouzi Lekjaa said construction of the Hassan II will be completed in early 2028. According to the IMF, Morocco intends to spend about $19 billion between 2024 and 2030 building airports, stadiums, hotels and a high-speed ⁠rail network, as well as a train station and highway to connect the stadium with Casablanca 45 km (28 miles) away.

Casablanca will need to work on its hotels to compete with Madrid and Barcelona after a FIFA technical report rated its accommodation offering for the general public at 3.1 compared to 5 for Spain.

It has been revealed that but a successful bid is not just about who has ‌the best stadium, hotels and transport. Often bids go to the country that would ​receive the greater benefit, Trade said.

In Morocco, the World Cup was an opportunity to expand railways and develop the whole Casablanca area, Lekjaa told state ‌broadcaster 2M. A Moroccan source familiar with the discussions remarked the final should go to the stadium with the largest ​capacity — and to an African country.

"It would be awkward – embarrassing, even – and would send the wrong message to Africa, one of the world's biggest producers of raw football talent, if the World Cup final were ultimately awarded to a non-African country with a smaller stadium," the person stated.

#117580. The summer that changed Welsh football

The summer that changed Welsh football

📅 04 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2278 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • "Walking to the ground in Bordeaux and what I find hilarious, in hindsight, is how low our expectations were.".
  • Wales had gone more than half a century without playing at a major tournament, so it was understandable that expectations were modest.
  • Generations of fans had been scarred by agonising near misses and downright dismal failures of the past so, when Wales finally realised a nation's dream by qualifying for Euro 2016, just being there was enough for many.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

"Walking to the ground in Bordeaux and what I find hilarious, in hindsight, is how low our expectations were.".

Wales had gone more than half a century without playing at a major tournament, so it was understandable that expectations were modest.

Generations of fans had been scarred by agonising near misses and downright dismal failures of the past so, when Wales finally realised a nation's dream by qualifying for Euro 2016, just being there was enough for many.

Bordeaux was bathed in sunshine on the afternoon of Saturday, 11 June, tens of thousands of Welsh supporters descending on the French city for their opening game against Slovakia.

Industry observers note that "We were all saying things like, 'Oh, the anthem's going to be good, that's guaranteed'. We could have lost 10-0 but they were definitely playing the anthem," the comedian and presenter tells BBC Sport Wales as part of Iconic: The Summer that Changed Welsh Football.

It has been revealed that an anthem heard at a major tournament for the first time in 58 years. Glorious catharsis to stir the soul.

Wales had ridden a wave of emotion to get there, a golden generation of players - Gareth Bale, Aaron Ramsey et al - scaling new heights under the guidance of their charismatic manager Chris Coleman.

"I was saying to all the players, 'Keep calm, don't act like we're too excited to be here'," Coleman recalls.

"But Bordeaux was like the centre of Cardiff, Welsh fans everywhere outside the hotel and, as soon as we were getting on the bus, I was chanting with the fans! I was like, 'What am I doing? Calm down'. I got lost in it.".

Sources indicate that coleman and his players eventually composed themselves. After a trademark Bale free-kick had put Wales in front, Hal Robson-Kanu came off the bench to score a late winner and send a nation into raptures.

"Euro 2016 was a turning point for Welsh football," says Ben Davies, the Tottenham Hotspur defender who made a crucial goalline block early in the game.

"There was so much talk about 1958 and I'd heard about it, I'd seen the odd clip about it, but it felt like a pipedream to actually have Wales in a major tournament.

"So to do it, forget about how well we did in it, just to even get to that tournament, it gave us a belief that it was possible.".

For those among the sea of red shirts in Bordeaux that day, it did not feel like life could get any better - but this was only the beginning.

This was the summer that would change Welsh football forever.

âIt was like being in the centre of Cardiff â there were Welsh fans everywhereâ.

Until Euro 2016, Wales' story had been dominated by tales of heartache, Joe Jordan's handball in 1977 and the Romania defeat of 1993 among many painful chapters.

But by getting to France, Wales freed themselves from that history.

"There had been some really low points for Wales, so to finally do that was a huge achievement," indicates Ramsey, the then Arsenal midfielder who would go on to be named in Uefa's team of the tournament.

Industry observers note that wales had momentum they had never felt before coming into the competition. Victory over Slovakia - and the prospect of getting to the second round - took that to another level.

A last-gasp defeat by England in Lens momentarily punctured that optimism, but the final group game against Russia presented Coleman's side with a chance to secure their place in the knockout stages.

This was meant to be nerve-wracking for a team with no major tournament experience against seasoned opponents.

But under a lilac sunset in Toulouse, Coleman's men played with a flair and verve unlike any other Wales side.

In a recent development, "That was our best performance," notes Coleman. "We were awesome.".

Wales cut Russia to ribbons with a breathtaking attacking display, racing into a 2-0 lead in 20 minutes.

After Ramsey's delicate finish put Wales in front, they poured forward with such gusto that even Neil Taylor scored - the wing-back's first goal since he was playing in non-league for Wrexham six years earlier.

"When Tayls scored, that summed up how things were falling for us," claims Joe Allen, who was exceptional in midfield that night.

"This was one of those once-in-a-lifetime moments you've got to capitalise on.".

That is exactly what Wales did. Bale added a third in the second half to become the tournament's top scorer at that point, and the winning margin could have been even wider.

Joe Ledley (right) dances in front of the Wales fans after the 3-0 win over Russia in Toulouse.

"We completely dominated them," says Joe Ledley, who ran the game alongside Allen in midfield.

As well as Ledley played, though, what elevated him to cult status was his post-match dancing in front of the Wales fans.

"I don't know where those moves came from," he grins. "I used to dance with my mates all the time at local pubs in Fairwater [in Cardiff]. I just went for it.".

Wales fans could scarcely believe what they had witnessed. Having already lived a dreamlike existence in France, this was starting to feel surreal.

The odyssey took them to Paris next, Wales' first knockout fixture since Pele had scored the only goal as Brazil beat them in a 1958 World Cup quarter-final.

This time, Coleman's men had the novelty of being favourites against an obdurate Northern Ireland side, who made life difficult for their opponents in a tense last-16 tie.

Bale eventually prised them open â his cross turned into his own net by Gareth McAuley â to set up a quarter-final against Belgium, and what would turn out to be the greatest night in Welsh football history.

'I remember like it was yesterday' - Euro 2016 hero Robson-Kanu.

Wales fans made a lasting impression in France, with their distinctive bucket hats and chant of 'Don't Take Me Home', which became an unofficial anthem of the Euros. Uefa even gave them an "outstanding contribution" award.

"What I loved about Welsh supporters at the Euros was we were just desperate to enjoy every second and suck the marrow out of it because we didn't know if it was going to happen again," says James.

"We're there to have fun. I'm not saying the result was secondary, but we all had realistic expectations.".

No wonder when you consider Wales' quarter-final opponents were Belgium, ranked number one in the world at the time with a squad boasting stellar talents such as Kevin de Bruyne, Romelu Lukaku and Eden Hazard.

"That Belgian side, on paper, was like a team to represent Earth against Mars," James adds. "It was like a team from space.".

It did not help matters that the game was essentially a home fixture for Belgium, whose fans filled the stadium in Lille, fewer than 10 miles from the Belgian border.

The odds were stacked against Coleman and his players, lengthening further when Radja Nainggolan's thunderous long-range strike gave Belgium an early lead.

But Wales believed they could win, not least because they had beaten Belgium in a qualifier in Cardiff 13 months earlier, and they responded magnificently as captain Ashley Williams headed in a deserved equaliser.

Then, nine minutes into the second half, Bale played a raking long ball to Ramsey, who found Robson-Kanu in the penalty area. And time stood still.

"I remember controlling the ball in the box and there was momentum carrying everyone away from the goal," Robson-Kanu states. "I just remember Cruyffing the entire opposition.".

With a manoeuvre as audacious as it was inspired, Robson-Kanu flummoxed three surrounding Belgian defenders with a Cruyff-turn before finishing supremely beyond Thibaut Courtois.

Wales' fans came to be known as the Red Wall during Euro 2016.

"It was an out-of-body experience," adds the forward, who was without a club at the time.

"Looking back, you realise careers are defined by moments, and to have a moment that you're truly remembered for is a real honour.".

Industry observers note that belgium pushed desperately for an equaliser but Sam Vokes headed in superbly to seal a 3-1 triumph. The celebrations were as ecstatic on the touchline as they were in the stands; disbelief as it dawned on players, staff and fans that Wales were heading to their first semi-final.

"There are certain moments in your life that are so good you wish you could just stop it and say, 'Let's just sit in this moment'," states Coleman.

"That was one of those moments. We got back in the dressing room and I can't describe the atmosphere.".

Allen, another Welshman in Uefa's team of the tournament, adds: "That's the moment where it crossed from being a good story into, 'This is more than anyone dreamed was possible'.".

The next, and what would prove to be the final, stop on Wales' magical ride was a semi-final against eventual champions Portugal in Lyon.

Shorn of the suspended Ramsey and Davies, Wales were stifled by their canny opponents, who secured a 2-0 win with second-half goals from Cristiano Ronaldo and Nani.

This was the end of the adventure in France, but the beginning of a glorious era for Welsh football.

"It was a really important moment for Wales, our history and generations to come," says Ramsey.

Having been absent from major tournaments for 58 years, Wales went on to qualify for a second successive European Championship, before achieving what Davies describes as the "holy grail" of reaching a first World Cup for 64 years in 2022.

"We opened the door that had been closed a long time," says Coleman.

The milestones kept coming, with the women's side qualifying for their first major tournament at Euro 2025.

Whereas Welsh national teams only used to dream of playing on the world's grandest stages, there is now an expectation they get there â and that stems from 2016.

Wales players and staff celebrate with their fans after their Euro 2016 quarter-final win over Belgium.

"With more money coming in from qualification for the European Championships, particularly Euro 2016, we ended up being more cash-rich," claims Jonathan Ford, chief executive of the Football Association of Wales (FAW) from 2009 to 2021.

In a recent development, "That enabled us to put more money across the board: women's football, grassroots football. We transformed the women's game.".

Uefa vice-president Laura McAllister is a former captain of Wales who played a leading role in getting the FAW to formally establish a national women's team in the 1990s.

"There was nothing inevitable about what happened post-2016 and that's why I think we should give credit to the FAW, and Jonathan Ford particularly, for steering us out of the tournament into that era," says McAllister.

Recent findings suggest that "I was part of the FAW Trust in 2016. I can remember times before that when Jonathan came into the board and noted things like, 'Until the men qualify for a major tournament, we can't invest in X, Y and Z'. And that included the women's national team.

"While I bristled at that because it felt unfair, the financial realities of the FAW meant until the men got to a position where they generated income from participating and winning, it was going to be impossible for us to deliver the strategy we had for Welsh football.".

McAllister travelled to France 10 years ago as a fan, and Qatar in 2022 to cheer on Wales' men at a World Cup.

When the women played at Euro 2025 in Switzerland, McAllister was there again to see the legacy not only of her own pioneering work in establishing the team but the far-reaching effects of 2016.

Industry observers note that "Something happens when you qualify. It's flicking a switch in mentality - it becomes something realistic and achievable," she adds.

"What matters far more is what you do with the breakthrough moment, not how you've performed.".

Wales' women are now trying to take the next step of qualifying for their first World Cup, while the men looked on enviously as their showpiece event happened without them in the United States, Canada and Mexico this summer.

Disappointing as it was, that frustration itself represented a shift in mindset that came after Euro 2016 â a sharp contrast to the passive acceptance that met Wales' previous absence from major tournaments.

Since that golden month in France, Wales feel like they belong at this level.

"The best thing we could give the teams coming after us was to say it's possible," indicates Coleman.

Subsequent qualifications have been the legacy of Euro 2016, while future ambitions are proof of a desire to ensure generations to come continue to build on the foundations laid by their predecessors.

There is plenty more Wales' men and women want to achieve but, whatever happens, there will never be another summer quite like Euro 2016.

"We're so proud of each other and what we achieved," notes Ledley.

Recent findings suggest that "Nobody thought we'd do it. When I walk down the street now, everyone says, 'Thank you for 2016, the best summer of my life'.".

Industry observers note that james can attest to that. "It remains the best month of my life," he says. "I don't think you often know it's the best month of your life as it's happening.".

With the benefit of hindsight, it is laughable to think you could find a Welsh football fan who would disagree.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, germany, who finished top of Group A2 following their 5-0 win over the Netherlands in Berlin on Monday are to face Belgium in the Nations League quarterfinals — after they finished second in Group A1. The Belgians recently came up with a statement result of their own, beating Italy 4-1. The match-up between the neighboring countries promises to be closely contested, with Belgium sitting at No. 8 in the men's rankings, three places above Germany.

The head coach of Belgium is former Bayern Munich player Mark van Bommel, who took over from Rudi Garcia following the World Cup, where they were knocked out by eventual champions Spain in the quarterfinals.

Germany head into the knockout phase on a high note, not only because they won their group, but also the way they performed in their last two matches, against Serbia and the Netherlands in the group stage.

Recent findings suggest that germany head coach Jürgen Klopp followed the draw, held in Nyon on Friday, from the German FA's (DFB) Frankfurt offices. He played down the notion that Germany enter the tie as the favorites.

"I've practically never given it any thought. It's never interested me," he noted.

Industry observers note that "An awful lot can happen in that time. We're very happy with the final impression we left, yet we're also fully aware that we're only at the very beginning of a development process. We want to carry this positive momentum forward—there's still a great deal to be done.".

The matches are slated for March 25 and March 30, 2027, and having won their group, Germany will have home-field advantage for the second leg.

Germany and Belgium have faced each other 26 times to date, with West Germany and Germany having the upper hand with 20 wins, five defeats and one draw.

Should Germany advance to the semifinals, they will go on to face the winner of England and Norway, a World Cup quarterfinals rematch.

In the other two semifinals matchups, the Netherlands drew Portugal, while the top pairing sees Spain face France in a rematch of one of last summer's World Cup semifinals.

The "Final Four" mini tournament is to be held from June 9 to 13 but the host venue won't be determined until the semifinal lineup has been completed.

Scientists should resist political pressure to provide certainty when the evidence suggests otherwise, notes Andy Stirling.Your browser does not support the audio element.Download MP3See transcript.

Science’s greatest failure is not getting things wrong, but by sometimes pretending that there is more certainty than there really is, says social scientist Andy Stirling.

This can happen, he states, when researchers face political pressure to provide a single, definitive answer, when the evidence is far more complex.

In the final episode of a six-part podcast series about failure in science, Stirling, an emeritus professor at the University of Sussex in Brighton, UK, draws on examples from climate change, the COVID-19 pandemic, environmental campaigns and energy policy.

“In those areas, science just does not convey the degree of uncertainty and of variability and of how many potentially viable options are being cut out when you just give one clear answer,” he claims. “It thinks it’s helping society by just giving one picture of the truth. And in fact, it’s undermining both itself and democracy when it does that.”.

Stirling, whose research includes science and technology policy and environmental politics, claims that on occasions politicians have almost literally hidden behind scientists on a podium, who have relied on their authority and expertise to protect them.

Earlier this year, Stirling spoke at a one-day conference on failure in science, with a focus on careers and innovation. It was held at Imperial College London in partnership with Nature.

"Owen was on the phone to the manager and his agent while I was in labour. They waited for me to give birth and then he went out on loan pretty much as soon as I was out of hospital.".

Industry observers note that owen Dale's loan deal wasn't to a local club, but to Portsmouth - a city more than 200 miles away. His partner, Jessica Beaumont, had never even been there.

Sources indicate that and the pair had only just got the keys to a house they had bought. They would end up staying in it for just one night.

"Since living together, we've moved five times in five years," states Jessica.

"You have to be prepared for anything in the transfer window. But it's also a really fortunate position to be in at a young age.".

This period - when clubs are permitted to buy, sell and loan players - takes place twice a year, in January and during the summer, for clubs in the Premier League, the English Football League (EFL) and the Women's Super League (WSL).

While a select few stay in one place throughout their career, for most players moving from club to club is just part of life in the modern game.

Sources indicate that jessica met Owen when he was at Crewe Alexandra. A move to Blackpool soon followed.

Industry observers note that "I didn't get together with him because he was a footballer so I never considered the footballer life - that he might just have to move at the last minute," she states. "We just met and we clicked.".

But it soon became apparent that dealing with almost constant uncertainty would be part of that life.

The move to Blackpool was a loan, with an option to buy, so for six months - during which Jessica was pregnant with their son Xavier - they did not know whether he would be staying there or heading back to Crewe.

Blackpool decided to sign Owen, but he was soon out on loan again. This isn't uncommon, with loan deals a way for clubs to help young prospects gain first-team experience and get regular playing time elsewhere.

"When the move to Portsmouth happened it really hit me - I had to quickly realise that 'OK this is now my life'," says Jessica.

Just before Owen's loan deal to Portsmouth the couple had bought their first house together in Congleton - a town close to Jessica's family in Stoke on Trent, and commutable to Blackpool.

"We spent one night in there - we hadn't even unpacked," she says.

They decided a 10-hour round trip on Owen's day off in the week to see his newborn son was not an option.

"We thought 'if he's not playing well because he's tired, what's the point in doing this'?" says Jessica, who adds that they ended up renting out the Congleton house and have been living in rented accommodation themselves ever since.

"I was finishing my law degree and had a job at the time - I had to say to them I wouldn't be coming back from maternity leave," she notes.

Post-natal complications also made it difficult for her to travel at the time.

"I had Owen on the phone basically saying, 'I've done a couple of house viewings. I've chosen this one. This is where we're going to be living' and showing me on FaceTime," she recalls.

"In that moment I did feel really out of control.".

Uprooting her life at short notice and leaving her family behind was challenging and Jessica remembers spending a lot of time alone in Portsmouth when Owen was at away games.

But she remembers lots of positives from that time too, including when she became friends with another player's partner.

"I was so fortunate that she would often stay with me when Owen was away," she claims.

"I say to her all the time that I'll appreciate that time forever because I was just so isolated.

"Our schedules were the same - when Owen went away her partner was also away - I didn't have to be fully alone and she got it.".

Owen made 28 appearances for Plymouth Argyle last season.

Owen, now 27, has played most of his career in League One, with two stints in the Championship when we was with Blackpool and Oxford United.

Recent findings suggest that last season was spent on loan at Plymouth Argyle and he is currently a free agent - this means he is not tied to any club by a legal contract. Owen can now join a newly introduced team without a transfer fee because no former employer owns his registration rights.

Many of his moves have been on deadline day and he notes he is "very aware of the sacrifices" his family make.

"There's always the risk that a move might not work," he states. "So I might uproot my whole family for this next venture and it all goes south.

"Over the years I've learned that until there's a contract signed on the dotted line, you could end up anywhere.".

Owen went on loan to Portsmouth in 2022 just days after Jessica gave birth to Xavier.

Owen returned to Blackpool the following year and made 32 appearances for the Tangerines.

The family moved to Bicester in 2024, as Owen helped Oxford United win promotion to the Championship.

Owen joined Wigan Athletic on loan the following year making his debut in a 2â1 FA Cup fourth-round defeat by Fulham.

Last season the family lived in Devon after Owen went on loan again - this time to Plymouth Argyle.

For now, Jessica's career in law is on hold, she instead has a job in social media and works from home.

She also posts about her experiences on TikTok, regularly using #wag and #waglife.

"My career can be picked up at any time - whereas his career is right now and you've really got to take every opportunity," she says.

"As much as people say it's a glamorous lifestyle you do make sacrifices so your partner can have their dream and get themselves as far as they can in football.

"At the end of the day, as much as I'm involved, it's his career. That means in order for me to support him properly I can't get emotionally involved.".

This includes not getting too emotionally attached to where they live.

"We usually rent newer houses that are a blank canvas so we can make them our own, although this last season the accommodation was provided furnished by Argyle," she indicates.

"We put a lot of Xavier's toys and garden stuff in storage and referred to our Plymouth accommodation as 'the holiday house'.

"It can be hard when he asks us to get things like his trampoline which we don't have with us.".

Owen's career is always the priority, Jessica says.

"When Owen was at Oxford he had one year left on his contract and I loved it there," she says.

Sources indicate that "But the best thing was for him to go and get game time somewhere miles away. So we moved.".

While Premier League footballers can earn tens of thousands of pounds a week - sometimes hundreds of thousands - life in the lower leagues can be very different.

"When you think 'Wag' [players' wives and girlfriends] and you think 'footballer', both of those terms come with this stereotype that our lives are easy," Jessica says.

"People also put League One players in the same bracket as Premier League players.

"In the Premier League they're often set up for life - we can't live in that way because we have to prepare for life after football.".

Adding to the uncertainty of where they will be playing is also the possibility or relegation or injury.

It has been revealed that "When we were at Portsmouth, Blackpool was still his parent club and they got relegated," states Jessica. "Owen wasn't even involved that season, but his wage was still affected.

Recent findings suggest that "You have to be prepared for everything. You just can't live outside of your means.

"But it's still a really fortunate position to be in.

"Luckily, Owen's been good with injuries. There are some players who they get injured in the last month of the season and they're out of contract.

"In football things can be really positive or really negative.".

The uncertainty also affects their children - four-year-old Xavier and two-month old Etta.

"Now that Xavier is growing up - he's fast approaching school age - another thing that will have to be added into the mix is his stability," says Jessica.

Even normal things like organising his recent fourth birthday party aren't always straightforward.

"We couldn't plan to have a party in Plymouth with balloons and cakes etc because we didn't know if we were going to be there," she notes.

"Instead we planned a party near my family in Stoke-on-Trent - we needed to make something work regardless of what happens with Owen's job.

"As much as I worry about Xavier and Etta, I also think how amazing it's going to be for them when they're older to be able to tell their life story and say they've lived in all these different places.

"I think it's teaching them a good life lesson that they don't need to be tied to one place.".

She says they have made every move a positive experience.

"We've said to Xavier that we might be moving soon and when we do we're going to get his bike back out of storage," says Jessica.

"That way he knows that moving is a possibility and hopefully he's not thinking about what he's going to lose but what he's going to gain.

Recent findings suggest that "The fortunate thing for us is that Xavier loves football. He gets a lot of excitement as well from the new strips and the new chants and all of that kind of thing.".

Xavier has enjoyed watching his dad play at each of his new clubs.

So, does Jessica have any tips for people in a similar situation?

"The main thing for me personally - and what I've learned first hand - is the importance of keeping your own identity outside of football," she says.

"If you get too wrapped up in it, it only puts more pressure on your partner.

"If you can get a hobby, a routine or even a work-from-home job, that can help - things that can move with you.".

Being sensible financially is also important.

"I'd also say that if you have a season where you get promoted, try not to change your lifestyle and to bank the promotion money so that you have as much stability as you can," she adds.

In a recent development, "In our house, I de-clutter maybe once a month," she states. "This helps me because I don't have control over Owen's career. But what I do have control over is making sure that if and when anything does happen, the house is ready to be packed up and moved.

"When it's the transfer window I will plan in one-week blocks - that gives me that little bit of certainty in a situation where I have no control.".

She admits "it can be hard" but "on the flip side it's so exciting".

"We've lived in places that we never would have lived in. And that's exciting for a relationship," she adds.

"You know, with some relationships you can get bored.

"In football, you don't get bored!".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

England defender John Stones faces a trial in 2028 after he allegedly missed a police speeding letter while playing at the World Cup.

The 32-year-old defender, who left Manchester City for Inter Milan in the summer, was caught driving his £150,000 Range Rover at 58mph through a 50mph zone of the M60 in March 2026.

Greater Manchester Police said Stones did not respond to two letters and on 27 April he was charged with failing to furnish driver information, which he has since pleaded not guilty to.

The central defender instructed Freeman & Co Solicitors to battle the claim – a firm owned by Nick Freeman, who has represented a string of celebrity clients in motoring offences and trademarked his tabloid moniker Mr Loophole.

Stones now faces trial on 29 September 2028 at Warrington Magistrates’ Court.

This comes after he was this year convicted of speeding and landed with a £1,052 court bill after he missed a police letter while at the World Cup with England.

In relation to the latest allegation, Stones has denied receiving the request for information from the police and asked prosecutors prove it was served.

In a letter to the court, his lawyers added: “It was not reasonably practicable for the defendant to give the information within the requisite period.”.

They also claimed GMP included “hearsay” in its single justice procedure notice dated 20 October.

Stones’s team requested that the trial last at least two hours and be heard in the morning.

They also asked permission to be excused from a pre-trial case management hearing, if such a date is required.

Stones was additionally caught driving his Range Rover at 43mph along a country lane near his Cheshire mansion in May.

He admitted being the driver when first contacted by Cheshire Police, but did not respond to a second letter offering him the chance to pay a fixed penalty to keep the speeding offence out of court.

He was then prosecuted and convicted in the single justice procedure, with a magistrate last week issuing him four penalty points and ordering him to pay a £666 fine, £120 in costs, and a £266 victim surcharge.

Explaining that mishap, Stones wrote to Warrington Magistrates Court to say: “Nothing to say about the speeding.

“The reason I am only responding to the offence now is because I represent our country for football and so I have not been home and seen any post.

“I sent off my letter on the 28th May to give my details, I went off to join England.

“We were there until the 19th July.

“I went on holiday and then moved to Milan, so this has been found by chance, as no-one has been home for almost four months.

“This is the reason I also would not be able to be present as I no longer am residing in the country.”.

Stones started the first match of the World Cup finals in the USA after being selected in the 26-man squad; he featured again in the quarter-final clash with Mexico and played in England’s semi-final defeat to Argentina.

The central defender, who played for Barnsley and Everton before a 10-year spell with Manchester City, has made four appearances so far for Inter Milan since his summer switch to the San Siro.

Breaking: 73 goals from dropping deep - we ask Kane to break down how he did it

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Harry Kane is one of the leading names in the race for this year's Ballon d'Or, having scored 73 goals last season for club and country.
  • As Harry Kane's career has progressed, the 33-year-old has taken an increasingly complete role, popping up to collect the ball as deep as his own box.
  • Many wonder why a talisman tasked with scoring doesn't spend more time closer to goal, but last season the England and Bayern Munich striker scored 73 goals - the highest tally of his career - while playing deeper than he ever has done.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Harry Kane is one of the leading names in the race for this year's Ballon d'Or, having scored 73 goals last season for club and country.

As Harry Kane's career has progressed, the 33-year-old has taken an increasingly complete role, popping up to collect the ball as deep as his own box.

Many wonder why a talisman tasked with scoring doesn't spend more time closer to goal, but last season the England and Bayern Munich striker scored 73 goals - the highest tally of his career - while playing deeper than he ever has done.

When I mention this paradox, a grin spreads across his face.

"Until you really understand football and understand what we've been talking about, it's so easy to say 'stay high, you're going to score' but it doesn't work like that," Kane notes.

I sat down to speak to Kane about the finer details of his game, shedding light on his unique role.

In a recent development, watching Kane train, his professionalism is palpable. England's record goalscorer is one of the first out on the pitch. The younger players indulge in playful kick-ups as he watches, engaged in conversation with a member of staff.

From a distance, that makes it easy to confuse him with a coach but, given his role on the pitch, it is a fitting mistake.

Kane's style of play reflects who he is as a person, with those who know him saying he is well-rounded and humble on and off the pitch.

How dropping deep helps Kane score.

Recent findings suggest that the season is in its infancy but Kane isn't basking in the success of the past 12 months. With only five days of pre-season training under his belt, the England captain completed 90 minutes of Bayern's 2-1 win over Borussia Dortmund to lift the German Super Cup.

Recent findings suggest that as demanding as his roaming role is, he has taken the physical demands of it in his stride. Across the past six seasons, STATSports - a sports technology company Kane has invested in - found his distance covered, high-speed running and accelerations were up 8%, 22% and 42% respectively.

And given how the tactical landscape has changed over that time, it is particularly impressive Kane has been able to not only keep up, but stay ahead.

Kane's role has evolved drastically over the past nine years, with the striker now heavily involved in all phases of the game -Â including as deep as his own box.

"Over the last five or six years, man-to-man pressure has become bigger," Kane says.

"European football is physical and top teams are trying to win the ball back high, trusting their defenders and midfielders to defend man for man to win their battles.".

Given that change, the best teams have recruited physical athletes and brilliant dribblers who can beat their man when the game becomes a series of one-against-ones.

Kane, not known for his dribbling - and by his own admission "not the fastest", has thrived on his own terms.

Against Dortmund, there was a specific moment Kane dropped deep, looking to arrive in space unmarked. Recognising the danger, two players converged on the Englishman.

Kane's dribbling is cerebral. His speed of thought provides him solutions to problems others would attempt to solve with their feet alone.

It has been revealed that after getting low and using his strength to shrug centre-back Waldemar Anton off him, Kane rose, slightly adjusting his body to the right. These micro-adjustments are a hallmark of his game and through them he is able to shift an entire team's momentum.

Fooled by this feint, Daniel Svensson and Jobe Bellingham found themselves wrong-footed as Kane snapped the ball back the other way, opening up the entire pitch from within Bayern's half.

Kane wins his individual battle with Waldemar Anton, shielding the ball and showcasing strength.

As he rises, he positions his body to the right, facing his own goal.

It has been revealed that through clever body positioning, Kane moves the opposition towards the right side of the pitch. This is his cue to cut the ball back into the open space.

This allows Kane to evade two defenders, now facing the opposition's goal.

Earlier this year, Bayern boss Vincent Kompany shed light on Kane's unique role, explaining it as being 50% coached and 50% Kane deciding what to do.

According to recent reports, "I think it's partly instinct, using my football brain and getting the feeling on the pitch," says Kane. "If, for example, I want to drop and see if the centre-back really wants to commit, he might commit into midfield, but is he going to commit if I drop all the way to my box?

"After the first five or 10 minutes you really get an understanding of how the opposition are going to play, which dictates how I play.".

In the second minute of Bayern Munich's game against Arsenal, Kane dropped deep into a position normally occupied by centre-backs. Arsenal centre-back William Saliba marked him all the way, vacating space higher up the pitch.

There is a shared understanding at Bayern of an approach that allows team-mates to make sense of rotations that, to the naked eye, appear random.

Kane, who is given more freedom than most, is at the centre of it.

Sources indicate that "I feel like my position now is as one of two 10s, and you work together," he says. "You can double up on one side to overload, which causes the opposition centre-backs a problem of who to mark.

"If they want to mark both, they've got to go man-to-man and then that leaves space for our wingers or full-backs to run into.

"It's posing all these questions to the opposition but, personally, I love having someone close to me who I can link with.".

Kane built his reputation playing as a lone number nine, so it is interesting to hear him identify instead as a number 10 -Â in a front two.

In a recent development, "When you're the number nine on your own you can get marked by two centre-backs and you struggle to get touches on the ball," he indicates. "You're relying on everyone else to find you with the ball.".

Showing Kane two clips from last season, I ask him to talk through what was going through his head.

"The thing with our formation is, as long as there's someone in each position, it doesn't really matter who it is. Lucho [Luis Diaz] in this clip is playing as one of those 10s.

"I've come off to try and create a bit of space and Lucho's gone through the centre.".

Sources indicate that distracted by Kane's dropping-deep movement, one of the opposition midfielders is pulled towards him. This creates space, allowing Joshua Kimmich to punch the ball through to Diaz.

"I think it's Serge [Gnabry] making the run in behind which takes the defenders back, which allows me and Lucho that space in between. Lucho lays it off and whenever I'm in that position, around 20-25 yards out, I'm always looking if I can get my shot off.".

It is one of many examples of Kane initially dropping deep before scoring.

According to recent reports, "By playing deep when the play develops, I end up coming into a number 10 spot when everyone's dropped," he says. "I can get shots off from the edge of the box, which is a big strength of mine, or I'm running off the back of players where no-one's picking me up - because the midfielder finds it hard to [track].".

Sources indicate that the Frankfurt midfielder notices Kane dropping deep. Recognising this danger, he moves towards him.

With Frankfurt's central midfielder pulled towards Kane, Luis Diaz is able to receive a pass between the lines. He forms a central front two with Kane. The wingers ahead of them, Serge Gnabry and Michael Olise, push the defensive line back.

Kane is found in space around the edge of the box and strikes the ball hard into the net.

The second clip is from Bayern's Champions League tie against Club Brugge.

Usually Kane is marked by an opposition centre-back, but the Belgian club give that responsibility to their holding midfielder -Â something he recognises and exploits.

Lennart Karl scores without Kane touching the ball, but the striker's involvement is undeniable.

"These are the little runs, again, not everyone sees," Kane explains. "With Jamal Musiala and Lenny, they're so good at receiving the ball and dribbling so there'll be times where I will actually stay higher and let those guys get on the ball a bit deeper, and I'll try and make runs in behind.

"Without changing my game too much, I try and complement the players around me.

"I know Lenny is so good in those pockets and when he gets there, I'm more thinking of running in behind because, one, he can play me in and I can go through on goal, or two, he can dribble with the ball and do exactly what happened here.

"As soon as Lenny gets in that pocket I make the run and not always to get the ball, sometimes it is just to drag the defender away.

"Now he's one-against-one with a centre-back in the middle of the pitch and that's dangerous for any centre-back.".

Recent findings suggest that karl receives the ball in the middle of the pitch. As seen in yellow, Kane is being marked by Club Brugge's holding midfielder, rather than any of the central defenders.

Kane, recognising this, makes a diagonal run in behind, pulling the opposition holding midfielder away from the centre of the pitch.

Karl drives with the ball into the space created by Kane before putting the ball into the top corner.

It has been revealed that with the Ballon d'Or announcement on the horizon, Kane's name is in the conversation, primarily for the sheer volume of goals he has scored. What is easier to miss in that debate is the rest of his game.

Kane plays for the team in each phase of the game across the entirety of the pitch, while at the same time producing extraordinary individual numbers that match the likes of Cristiano Ronaldo, Lionel Messi and Erling Haaland.

He has described himself as playing in the role of a number 10, nine and six at times.

In a football world of specific and heavily drilled tactical roles, that is quite the achievement.
