Tech Report: Russia is developing a nuclear space weapon, US intelligence report finds

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1141 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that last month, the U.S.
  • In a recent development, the new report focuses on China, Russia and the emerging space powers of Iran and North Korea.
  • Sources indicate that the report — the 2026 edition of "Challenges to Security in Space" — is the third iteration of the DIA's unclassified intelligence assessment on space-related challenges and threats to U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that last month, the U.S. Defense Intelligence Agency (DIA) released a chilling and info-packed report judging the scope and breadth of threats posed by the nation's adversaries in space.

In a recent development, the new report focuses on China, Russia and the emerging space powers of Iran and North Korea. It looks at what's happening in Earth orbit and beyond, including cislunar space, the region between our planet and the moon.

Sources indicate that the report — the 2026 edition of "Challenges to Security in Space" — is the third iteration of the DIA's unclassified intelligence assessment on space-related challenges and threats to U.S. national security, as well as the extent to which space is treated internationally as a warfighting domain.

Sources indicate that information within the report, which you can read here, is current as of July 2026. DIA's mission is to provide intelligence on foreign militaries to help prevent wars, and win the ones that are fought.

The report's up-front finding is that China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea are developing, testing, deploying and using space capabilities "in a way that threatens the security of all space systems and their associated space benefits.".

Indeed, China and Russia are developing "a formidable spectrum" of offensive capabilities to degrade or destroy space services of other countries, from kinetic destruction to sophisticated jamming and cyber operations.

The DIA report also notes that "the production of cheaper, smaller, and simpler satellites, which are faster to develop and deploy, along with the expansion of commercially available launch services, are driving the rapid integration of commercial space alternatives to support national security.".

While space commercialization is making previously government-centered space services widely available to interested parties, the DIA report adds, that availability also includes state and non-state actors with malign interests.

A major item dealt with by the DIA is "counterspace" — and it's not the kind that you'll find in your kitchen.

Counterspace operations can be either offensive or defensive. They can be used on purpose to reversibly or irreversibly deny, disrupt, degrade, damage or destroy a space object or component of a space system.

Here are the key elements of counterspace, as identified within the DIA report:.

The DIA report underscores that Russia is developing a satellite designed to carry a nuclear weapon.

Russia is doing so despite its obligation to comply with the 1967 Outer Space Treaty. That U.N. agreement prohibits the placement of any objects carrying nuclear weapons, or any other kinds of weapons of mass destruction, into orbit around Earth.

"A space-based capability such as this could cause rapid and sudden loss or degradation of thousands of satellites operated by countries and companies around the world," the DIA report states, "as well as to the vital communications, navigation, scientific, meteorological, commercial and national security services they provide.".

A nuclear detonation in space could be tailored to impact satellites in most orbits, the DIA report warns, from low Earth orbit for commercial and reconnaissance satellites, geosynchronous orbit for critical communications, and medium Earth orbit for navigation and timing satellites.

The newly issued DIA report also observes that exploring cislunar space is of increasing interest to spacefaring nations for potential scientific and economic opportunities. However, nations such as China "may be exploring military applications from cislunar space," the report notes.

China has stated its goal of developing a cislunar space economy by 2045.

Sources indicate that "China is also the first country to attempt sustained operations on the far side of the moon, with numerous projects slated to support that effort through the next decade. China portrays its interest in cislunar space as peaceful, but PRC [People's Republic of China] officials have also discussed pursuing military capabilities in cislunar space," the report states.

Placing a keen eye on the DIA report is Peter Garretson, a senior fellow in defense studies at the American Foreign Policy Council and a strategy consultant who focuses on space and defense.

According to Garretson, the most significant positive change from earlier DIA appraisals is the explicit assessment that Russia is developing a satellite designed to carry a nuclear weapon. He told Space.com that the DIA's expanded treatment of the threat of a nuclear weapon on orbit reflects concerns in the Congress and the Trump White House.

However, Garretson also flagged what he noted is a consequential omission in the report: the disappearance of the prior treatment (in the 2022 version of the report) of research competition, surveillance beyond geosynchronous Earth orbit and the potential military use of deep space for staging reserve forces.

In Garretson's view, the DIA needs to help put the puzzle pieces together for Congress and the attentive public about what exactly China is doing, and how it fits together in the nation's strategy to achieve comprehensive space dominance.

According to Garretson, "everything they are doing, from launch cadence, reusable launch, commercial space investment, investments in power, propulsion, repair, manufacturing, to commercial assets working together" supports both an economic expansion toward new resources and what China hopes will be overwhelming military power and strategic depth.

Garretson senses the moves by China to develop extractive and in-space industries "is truly the strategic threat that could crush American space power. Now is the time to be making the investments to ensure we have a 'freedom's forge' and 'arsenal of democracy' in space that can protect the open space commerce that is the nation's strategy.".

As for the DIA's outlook for the future: The agency concluded that space almost certainly will remain an increasingly competitive and crowded environment as space capabilities improve and other countries seize opportunities in the final frontier.

"The increase of Chinese, Russian, Iranian and North Korean counterspace capabilities, rapid growth in the number of space objects, and the proliferation of requirements for space-enabled services," the DIA report states, "will all complicate operations in space in the coming decade.".

In a recent development, leonard David is an award-winning space journalist who has been reporting on space activities for more than 50 years. Currently writing as Space.com's Space Insider Columnist among his other projects, Leonard has authored numerous books on space exploration, Mars missions and more, with his latest being "Moon Rush: The Fresh Space Race" published in 2019 by National Geographic. He also wrote "Mars: Our Future on the Red Planet" released in 2016 by National Geographic. Leonard  has served as a correspondent for SpaceNews, Scientific American and Aerospace America for the AIAA. He has received many awards, including the first Ordway Award for Sustained Excellence in Spaceflight History in 2015 at the AAS Wernher von Braun Memorial Symposium. Following Real Madrid's turnaround victory against PSV Eindhoven in the Champions League, Jose Mourinho revealed his unusual half-time team talk that sparked his team’s second-half onslaught.

Asked how he inspired his side after trailing 1-0 at the Santiago Bernabeu Stadium on Tuesday, Mourinho initially wanted to keep his methods under wraps as he joked: "The locker room is like (Las) Vegas, what happens in Vegas stays in Vegas,".

Jude Bellingham, introduced as a substitute to spark the Madrid attack, later admitted the manager was understandably "a bit angry" following a disappointing opening period.

In a recent development, rather than relying solely on a dressing-room row, Mourinho selected images to highlight his side’s positional mistakes. The tactical correction paid immediate dividends, with Madrid scoring five unanswered goals after the break to secure a 5-1 win, maintaining a perfect record with five consecutive European victories this term.

Recent findings suggest that "I saw a terrible first half and tried with the analysts to find three or four images that could show the players exactly what we were doing wrong," Mourinho explained. "It was a half time with few words because a picture is worth a thousand words. We looked at three different images, one from a defensive perspective and two from an offensive perspective. I think with visualisation, it’s much easier for the players to understand.".

In a recent development, the manager noted that the visual breakdown prompted an immediate "mental click" across the squad. Goalkeeper Thibaut Courtois agreed, adding: "On the screen you could see clearly that we weren’t doing things right and they were,".

Sources indicate that mourinho reshuffled his line-up drastically at the interval, making three changes including a double swap in central defence and introducing Bellingham, who had been rested from the start. The England midfielder’s arrival "proved key" to the outcome as he scored once and assisted another, with his manager noting he "gave the team a completely different dynamic.".

Federico Valverde levelled the score five minutes after the restart, before Bellingham produced a striking effort 10 minutes later to put Madrid ahead. Kylian Mbappé then struck twice before Vinícius Júnior wrapped up the scoring late on, assisted by Bellingham.

Before the interval, PSV had exploited Madrid's defensive gaps through swift counter-attacks, alarming the home fans - including newly appointed board member Rafael Nadal and his son - as the Dutch visitors created repeated openings.

To fix the defensive frailties, Mourinho withdrew Éder Militão and Antonio Rüdiger for Dean Huijsen and Ibrahima Konaté, while Bellingham replaced Aurélien Tchouaméni. He also adjusted the tactical roles of Arda Güler and Bernardo Silva.

Sources indicate that "The players at the back also felt much more comfortable pressing high," Mourinho remarked. "PSV gave us a hard time in the first half, and we struggled to win the ball back. In the second half, we had absolute control, and when the players up front wake up and start playing with joy, what happened can happen.".

Mbappé’s double made him the second-youngest player to reach 75 Champions League goals after Lionel Messi, reaching the mark in 103 games - the third-fastest behind Messi and Robert Lewandowski, according to Uefa statistics.

Meanwhile, Vinícius scored his 87th-minute strike to record just his second goal of the campaign for Madrid, and his first since August.

#117536. The haunting Masters meltdown that changed Rory McIlroy's career

The haunting Masters meltdown that changed Rory McIlroy's career

📅 03 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1591 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNN

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • Slumped on his club, head buried in his arm, Rory McIlroy looked on the verge of tears.
  • The then-21-year-old had just watched his ball sink into the waters of Rae’s Creek at Augusta National and with it, his dream of winning The Masters, a dream that had looked so tantalizingly close mere hours earlier.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Editor’s Note:  This story was originally published in April 2023.

Slumped on his club, head buried in his arm, Rory McIlroy looked on the verge of tears.

The then-21-year-old had just watched his ball sink into the waters of Rae’s Creek at Augusta National and with it, his dream of winning The Masters, a dream that had looked so tantalizingly close mere hours earlier.

As a four-time major winner and one of the most decorated names in the sport’s history, few players would turn down the chance to swap places with McIlroy heading into Augusta this week.

Yet on Sunday afternoon of April 10, 2011, not a golfer in the world would have wished to be in the Northern Irishman’s shoes.

A fresh-faced, mop-headed McIlroy had touched down in Georgia for the first major of the season with a reputation as the leading light of the next generation of stars.

An excellent 2010 had marked his best season since turning pro three years earlier, highlighted by a first PGA Tour win at the Quail Hollow Championship and a crucial contribution to Team Europe’s triumph at the Ryder Cup.

Yet despite a pair of impressive top-three finishes at the Open and PGA Championship respectively, a disappointing missed cut at The Masters – his first at a major – served as ominous foreshadowing.

McIlroy shot 74 and 77 to fall four strokes short of the cut line at seven-over par, a performance that concerned him enough to take a brief sabbatical from competition.

But one year on in 2011, any lingering Masters demons looked to have been exorcised as McIlroy flew round the Augusta fairways.

Having opened with a bogey-free seven-under 65 – the first time he had ever shot in the 60s at the major – McIlroy pulled ahead from Spanish first round co-leader Alvaro Quirós with a second round 69.

It sent him into the weekend holding a two-shot cushion over Australia’s Jason Day, with Tiger Woods a further stroke behind and back in the hunt for a 15th major after a surging second round 66.

Sources indicate that and yet the 21-year-old leader looked perfectly at ease with having a target on his back. Even after a tentative start to the third round, McIlroy rallied with three birdies across the closing six holes to stretch his lead to four strokes heading into Sunday.

Sources indicate that the youngster was out on his own ahead of a bunched chasing pack comprising Day, Ángel Cabrera, K.J. Choi and Charl Schwartzel. After 54 holes, McIlroy had shot just three bogeys.

“It’s a great position to be in … I’m finally feeling comfortable on this golf course,” McIlroy told reporters.

It has been revealed that “I’m not getting ahead of myself, I know how leads can dwindle away very quickly. I have to go out there, not take anything for granted and go out and play as hard as I’ve played the last three days. If I can do that, hopefully things will go my way.

“We’ll see what happens tomorrow because four shots on this golf course isn’t that much.”.

The truth can hurt, and McIlroy was about to prove his assessment of Augusta to be true in the most excruciating way imaginable.

His fourth bogey of the week arrived immediately. Having admitted to expecting some nerves at the first tee, McIlroy sparked a booming opening drive down the fairway, only to miss his putt from five feet.

Three consecutive pars steadied the ship, but Schwartzel had the wind in his sails. A blistering birdie, par, eagle start had seen him draw level at the summit after his third hole.

A subsequent bogey from the South African slowed his charge, as McIlroy clung onto a one-shot lead at the turn from Schwartzel, Cabrera, Choi, and a rampaging Woods, who shot five birdies and an eagle across the front nine to send Augusta into a frenzy.

Despite his dwindling advantage and the raucous Tiger-mania din ahead of him, McIlroy had responded well to another bogey at the 5th hole, draining a brilliant 20-foot putt at the 7th to restore his lead.

The fist pump that followed marked the high-water point of McIlroy’s round, as a sliding start accelerated into full-blown free-fall at the par-four 10th hole.

His tee shot went careening into a tree, ricocheting to settle between the white cabins that separate the main course from the adjacent par-three course. It offered viewers a glimpse at a part of Augusta rarely seen on broadcast, followed by pictures of McIlroy anxiously peering out from behind a tree to track his follow-up shot.

Though his initial escape was successful, yet another collision with a tree and a two-putt on the green saw a stunned McIlroy eventually tap in for a triple bogey. Having led the field one hole and seven shots earlier, he arrived at the 11th tee in seventh.

By the time his tee drive at the 13th plopped into the creek, all thoughts of who might be the recipient of the green jacket had long-since switched away from the anguished youngster. It had taken him seven putts to navigate the previous two greens, as a bogey and a double bogey dropped him to five-under – the score he had held after just 11 holes of the tournament.

Mercifully, the last five holes passed without major incident. A missed putt for birdie from five feet at the final hole summed up McIlroy’s day, though he was given a rousing reception as he left the green.

Mere minutes earlier, the same crowd had erupted as Schwartzel sunk his fourth consecutive birdie to seal his first major title. After starting the day four shots adrift of McIlroy, the South African finished 10 shots ahead of him, and two ahead of second-placed Australian duo Jason Day and Adam Scott.

McIlroy’s eight-over 80 marked the highest score of the round. Having headlined the leaderboard for most of the week, he finished tied-15th.

Tears would flow during a phone call with his parents the following morning, but at his press conference, McIlroy was upbeat.

“I’m very disappointed at the minute, and I’m sure I will be for the next few days, but I’ll get over it,” he stated.

“I was leading this golf tournament with nine holes to go, and I just unraveled … It’s a Sunday at a major, what it can do.

“This is my first experience at it, and hopefully the next time I’m in this position I’ll be able to handle it a little better. I didn’t handle it particularly well today obviously, but it was a character-building day … I’ll come out stronger for it.”.

Once again, McIlroy would be proven right.

Sources indicate that just eight weeks later in June, McIlroy rampaged to an eight-shot victory at the US Open. Records tumbled in his wake at Congressional, as he shot a tournament record 16-under 268 to become the youngest major winner since Tiger Woods at The Masters in 1997.

Industry observers note that the historic victory kickstarted a golden era for McIlroy. After coasting to another eight-shot win at the PGA Championship in 2012, McIlroy became only the third golfer since 1934 to win three majors by the age of 25 with triumph at the 2014 Open Championship.

Before the year was out, he would add his fourth major title with another PGA Championship win.

And much of it was owed to that fateful afternoon at Augusta. In an interview with the BBC in 2015, McIlroy dubbed it “the most vital day” of his career.

“If I had not had the whole unravelling, if I had just made a couple of bogeys coming down the stretch and lost by one, I would not have learned as much.

In a recent development, “Luckily, it did not take me long to get into a position like that again when I was leading a major and I was able to get over the line quite comfortably. It was a huge learning curve for me and I needed it, and thankfully I have been able to move on to bigger and better things.

“Looking back on what happened in 2011, it doesn’t seem as bad when you have four majors on your mantelpiece.”.

McIlroy’s contentment came with a caveat: it would be “unthinkable” if he did not win The Masters in his career.

Yet as he prepares for his 15th appearance at Augusta National this week, a green jacket remains an elusive missing item from his wardrobe.

Despite seven top-10 finishes in his past 10 Masters outings, the trophy remains the only thing separating McIlroy from joining the ranks of golf immortals to have completed golf’s career grand slam of all four majors in the modern era: Gene Sarazen, Ben Hogan, Gary Player, Jack Nicklaus, and Tiger Woods.

A runner-up finish to Scottie Scheffler last year marked McIlroy’s best finish at Augusta, yet arguably 2011 remains the closest he has ever been to victory. A slow start in 2022 meant McIlroy had begun Sunday’s deciding round 10 shots adrift of the American, who teed off for his final hole with a five-shot lead despite McIlroy’s brilliant 64 finish.

Rory McIlroy: I will win the Masters.

Sources indicate that at 33 years old, time is still on his side. Though 2022 extended his major drought to eight years, it featured arguably his best golf since that golden season in 2014.

And as McIlroy knows better than most, things can change quickly at Augusta National.

The world has a golden chance to improve HIV prevention: don’t squander it

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1250 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • South Africa’s health officials at the launch in June of lenacapavir, a drug that provides strong protection against HIV when administered twice a year.Credit: Per-Anders Pettersson/Getty.
  • Sources indicate that earlier this month, the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved a generic version of the HIV drug lenacapavir for use as a preventive treatment.
  • A powerful HIV vaccine is finally within reach — thanks to these super antibodies.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

South Africa’s health officials at the launch in June of lenacapavir, a drug that provides strong protection against HIV when administered twice a year.Credit: Per-Anders Pettersson/Getty.

Sources indicate that earlier this month, the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved a generic version of the HIV drug lenacapavir for use as a preventive treatment. Twice-yearly injections of this game-changing medicine — originally developed by the organization Gilead Sciences in Foster City, California — have been shown to be more than 95% effective at preventing HIV acquisition1. At the same time, as Nature reports in a News feature, an HIV vaccine — that would ultimately be a more robust solution to preventing HIV — is closer than ever before.

A powerful HIV vaccine is finally within reach — thanks to these super antibodies.

A powerful HIV vaccine is finally within reach — thanks to these super antibodies.

It has been revealed that in 2024, Gilead signed licensing agreements with six pharmaceutical companies, allowing them to make and sell generic versions of lenacapavir in 120 low- and middle-income countries, subject to regulatory approval. The recent FDA approval brings access a step closer in these countries. The cost to consumers has been set at US$40 per year, fuelling hopes that the drug will help to bring the global HIV epidemic under control.

In a recent development, these welcome developments contrast with the situation of public funding for HIV research and treatment, which is reeling from deep and unconscionable cuts from the US government. Many of the researchers whom Nature spoke to for the News feature had been funded by a programme for preclinical HIV-vaccine research run by the US National Institutes of Health (NIH). But the agency ended the programme last year, forcing researchers to scale back their research and seek alternative funding. Whatever funding comes next is likely to be less stable and less predictable than the NIH funding. It’s imperative that the cuts be reversed — or new government funding sources found.

According to recent reports, the path to an HIV vaccine has been long and bumpy, with decades of high-profile and costly failures, but there is now light at the end of the tunnel. The latest strategy — known as germline targeting — is designed to trigger the production of rare, highly potent antibodies that can prevent infection with diverse HIV strains. The technique has shown encouraging results in animal models2–4 and in early trials in humans5. Researchers are more optimistic than they’ve been in years that an effective HIV vaccine could be on the horizon.

The end of AIDS is in sight: don’t abandon PEPFAR now.

The end of AIDS is in sight: don’t abandon PEPFAR now.

Industry observers note that but in the meantime, antiretroviral drugs such as lenacapavir look poised to have a major impact on infection prevention. In Africa alone, newly introduced infections could be cut by around one-third if just 5% of adults most likely to acquire HIV received the drug, and by half if it was given to one-fifth of adults, according to the Gates Foundation’s Institute for Disease Modelling in Seattle, Washington.

But lenacapavir alone is unlikely to bring the HIV epidemic fully under control. There are several reasons for this: first, it’s not always easy to determine who needs the drug most. Second, to be effective, the drug must be taken for most of someone’s life — or at least while they are sexually active. Third, even $40 a year is unaffordable for people on the very lowest incomes.

Until recently, the United States was the stand-out funder for antiretroviral drugs for people living with HIV in low-and middle-income countries. That stopped in January 2025, when the US administration suspended funding. Although it later restored a limited amount, the effects have been devastating. A survey published earlier this year found that some 1,700 facilities previously offering treatments to people living with HIV had closed as a result (see go.nature.com/4a7ftp4).

Trump blew up the global fight against AIDS. Can it recover?

Trump blew up the global fight against AIDS. Can it recover?

Sources indicate that such instability highlights the importance of vaccines. “The funding cuts that happened in the past couple of years have really made it even more obvious how fragile that system of reliance” on drug access is, claims Penny Moore, a virologist at South Africa’s National Institute for Communicable Disease in Johannesburg. And that fragility, as Rogier Sanders, an HIV-vaccine researcher at Amsterdam University Medical Centre, says, is why research into a vaccine remains a priority: “A vaccine makes you independent from access to drugs.”.

But the US cuts have not only curtailed the preclinical vaccine programme, they have also forced the postponement and scaling back of an HIV vaccine trial in South Africa. They have also affected supporting research, such as surveillance efforts tracking HIV evolution in African countries, claims Nairobi-based Vincent Muturi-Kioi, who is leading development of HIV vaccines at the International AIDS Vaccine Initiative in New York City.

Success stories such as the repurposing of lenacapavir as a preventive treatment and progress in vaccine development show the importance of investment in health. It is imperative that HIV vaccine research and deployment continues to receive support, at the same time as rolling out lenacapavir as widely as possible.

It could take more than a decade to translate the encouraging results with germline targeting into an effective HIV vaccine, and the current strategy might encounter more hurdles.

In a recent development, the world is closer than it has ever been to an effective HIV vaccine and has a drug capable of preventing infections. Now is the time for funders to ramp up investment, not cut it back.

Breaking: COP31: No agreement on climate science, disinformation spreading

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (974 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The annual UN climate conference is the place where countries negotiate the world's intends to limit global warming and adapt to its consequences — and who will pay for climate action as well as damage from storms, floods and droughts.
  • But this year at COP31 in Antalya, an ongoing dispute over the timing of a key assessment of global warming is risking the scientific foundations of global climate action, say observers.
  • "We are extremely concerned about the situation," stated a diplomat with the European delegation who could not speak on the record, adding that it came down to the future of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), the world's leading body of climate scientists.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The annual UN climate conference is the place where countries negotiate the world's intends to limit global warming and adapt to its consequences — and who will pay for climate action as well as damage from storms, floods and droughts.

But this year at COP31 in Antalya, an ongoing dispute over the timing of a key assessment of global warming is risking the scientific foundations of global climate action, say observers.

"We are extremely concerned about the situation," stated a diplomat with the European delegation who could not speak on the record, adding that it came down to the future of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), the world's leading body of climate scientists.

Recent findings suggest that the IPCC's scientific assessments, published every six to seven years, provide the basis for major international climate agreements, including the 2015 Paris Agreement. The IPCC began evaluating the latest climate science in 1988 and its most recent report was published in 2023.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Researchers should have actually already started work on the next edition but the last plenary session was put on hold in October at the urging of Russia, Iran, Saudi Arabia and Kenya.

According to recent reports, "The IPCC finds itself in a difficult situation," a spokesperson from the German Environment Ministry told DW at COP. "We stand ready to help resolve this issue, so that the panel can continue its work. To that end, we are holding many discussions with various countries to explore possible solutions.".

At the core of the dispute is the question of whether future UN climate talks base their negotiations on the latest scientific knowledge — or not.

That's especially relevant for the next "global stocktake," due in 2028, a report card on the world's climate efforts, which will shape action plans for countries around the world to lower planet-heating greenhouse gas emissions.

According to recent reports, the European Union, Brazil, the United Kingdom, small island states and several other countries especially at risk of the effects of climate change have called for the IPCC's seventh assessment report to be published in 2028, so it can be used to inform next steps for climate action. The report covers climate protection and impact.

"It's much more difficult without these scientific reports. Otherwise, we're just talking to ourselves or relying on information that's no longer current," mentioned a delegation source.

But Russia, Iran, India and Saudi Arabia want the IPCC report postponed until 2029, after the global stocktake.

The official reason: the tight timeline would be detrimental to the quality of the research, and could hinder the participation of researchers and governments representing developing countries.

Disagreements over budget issues have also held up the IPCC's work. Among other expenses, the funds are used to pay the travel arrangements for the hundreds of volunteer scientists, especially those from poorer countries, to attend the IPCC sessions.

"No budget means no more IPCC," stated a member from another delegation, also speaking on condition of anonymity.

It hasn't come to that point yet, but without planning certainty the whole process risks being delayed — along with the climate negotiations that depend on this knowledge.

Researchers with the IPCC, however, have said the timeline is attainable.

Industry observers note that "We have no time to lose," stated an open letter released in October signed by more than 100 researchers from 36 countries — including India and China. "We stand committed to continue working to deliver the [seventh assessment report] in a manner that is rigorous, timely and inclusive.".

But while the dispute over the timeline won't alter the scientific findings themselves, it could delay their political impact.

In its pre-COP communications, France accused the countries delaying the report's publication schedule of attempting to "obstruct science in order to lower the ambition of the global stocktake.".

The IPCC isn't a stranger to attempts at political persuasion: At past climate conferences, delegates from many countries have regularly negotiated the exact phrasing of the summary reports intended for policymakers.

Speaking at COP31 on November 17, EU Climate Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra said it was "fundamental to protect the integrity of climate science and the role of the IPCC as the source of best available science.".

Although there is no vote on the IPCC at COP31, it's possible that its significance and a timeline for the next report will be included in the final declaration of the climate talks, expected this weekend.

Sources indicate that the IPCC has been warning for years that disinformation is hindering global climate action. And the struggle for information and control over the narrative in Antalya hasn't just been limited to the IPCC.

This was apparent in a document DW obtained that had been sent anonymously to several less wealthy countries' delegations in the run-up to COP31.

It claimed to explain the nature of Turkey's proposed goals for boosting electrification to 35% by 2035, but went on to misrepresent several core details of the aims to make them seem less appealing to developing countries than they are in reality.

At least two countries confirmed to DW that they had received the document. It did not state where it hailed from and was labeled as an "equity assessment.".

The presentation portrays electrification as a business venture undertaken by wealthy countries at the expense of poorer nations. The International Energy Agency, however, has calculated that developing countries could save around $100 billion (€90 billion) in fossil fuel imports by 2035 through electrification.

The presentation also gives the impression that all countries must meet fixed electrification targets. In fact, according to the UN, the 35% target represents a global goal, with individual countries free to determine their own national pathways.

#117531. Could an ancient solar eclipse rewrite Egyptian history?

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1015 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Space ↗ Open Full Page

Could an ancient solar eclipse rewrite Egyptian history?

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1015 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The solar system is a clock that can be run in both directions.
  • Industry observers note that we know when it will happen because we can calculate the motions of Earth and the moon centuries in advance.
  • In a recent development, astronomers can reconstruct where the moon's shadow fell thousands of years ago, even when nobody left a record of it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The solar system is a clock that can be run in both directions. On Aug. 2, 2027, that clock will bring the moon's dark central shadow — a path of totality — back to Egypt. A total solar eclipse will sweep across the country, passing directly over Luxor and plunging some of ancient Egypt's greatest surviving monuments into darkness. Totality will begin in Luxor at approximately 1:02 p.m. EEST and last 6 minutes 22 seconds, according to Time and Date.

Industry observers note that we know when it will happen because we can calculate the motions of Earth and the moon centuries in advance. But run the same celestial clock backward and eclipses become one of nature's most precise timestamps.

In a recent development, astronomers can reconstruct where the moon's shadow fell thousands of years ago, even when nobody left a record of it. When an ancient text reliably describes an eclipse, it can anchor a moment in history to a specific place and time.

We know from astronomical calculations that eclipses crossed Egypt long before anyone left an identifiable written record of one. On April 1, 2471 B.C., a total solar eclipse swept across northern Egypt during the age of the great pyramid builders. In research published in 2025, archaeoastronomer Giulio Magli at the Polytechnic University of Milan proposed that the eclipse may help explain why Pharaoh Shepseskaf broke with tradition and built a huge rectangular tomb at South Saqqara instead of a pyramid. It's a tantalizing hypothesis, but no surviving Egyptian text records the eclipse.

According to recent reports, astronomers can calculate that an eclipse happened, but using it as a historical timestamp requires evidence that someone actually saw it and recorded it. That's where an eclipse almost 1,300 years later becomes particularly intriguing.

A passage in the Old Testament book of Joshua describes the sun and moon as if they stopped in the sky. After leading the people of Israel into Canaan — modern-day Israel and Palestine — Joshua prayed: "Sun, stand still at Gibeon, and moon, in the Valley of Aijalon. And the sun stood still, and the moon stopped, until the nation took vengeance on their enemies." Ancient Gibeon is about six miles (10 kilometers) northwest of Jerusalem.

In research published in 2017, researchers Colin Humphreys and Graeme Waddington at Cambridge University in the U.K. claimed it could refer to an annular solar eclipse on Oct. 30, 1207 B.C. It's a controversial interpretation, not least because it depends on exactly how the ancient Hebrew text is translated. However, if correct, it could be the oldest recorded solar eclipse with a date that has been identified — and it could also more accurately date the reign of Ramesses II. Also known as Ramesses the Great, he reigned for 66 years during Egypt's New Kingdom, commissioned Abu Simbel, made major additions to Karnak and Luxor Temple, and lived to be over 90. His reign marked the final peak of ancient Egyptian imperial power. According to the BBC, he is the "Jupiter" of the pharaonic system. However, the precise dates of his reign remain subject to debate, with historians using a combination of archaeological, historical and astronomical evidence to reconstruct the chronology.

In a recent development, now in the Egyptian Museum in Cairo, the Merneptah Stele is a large inscribed granite monument written in the fifth year of Pharaoh Merneptah's reign, successor to Ramesses II. Discovered in 1896 at Merneptah's mortuary temple on the west bank of the Nile, opposite modern-day Luxor, it describes an Egyptian military campaign in Canaan and mentions Israelites. Egyptologists generally date Merneptah's reign to around 1213 — 1203 B.C., placing his fifth year around 1209/1208 B.C. That means the Israelites were already living in Canaan by then.

Recent findings suggest that using calculations that accounted for changes in Earth's rotation over thousands of years, Humphreys and Waddington identified an annular eclipse visible from Canaan for five minutes on the afternoon of Oct. 30, 1207 B.C. If the biblical passage does describe this event, that's a fixed astronomical date that could be used to refine the chronology of the Egyptian pharaohs. The researchers proposed that it occurred during the second, third or fourth year of Merneptah's reign.

Recent findings suggest that if Humphreys and Waddington's interpretation of the biblical text is correct, the eclipse of 1207 B.C. could be the oldest solar eclipse identified in a written record. The researchers propose that Ramesses II reigned from approximately 1276 to 1210, with an uncertainty of about a year, slightly different from the conventional dates of 1279-1213 B.C. used by the British Museum.

It has been revealed that so an eclipse can be like a timestamp on an undated photograph, but this one does not show that the book of Joshua actually describes an eclipse. The interpretation of the Hebrew has been challenged by Marinus Anthony van der Sluijs, whose paper argues that the biblical narrative states that the sun was standing over Gibeon and the moon was over the Valley of Aijalon simultaneously — so not an eclipse at all.

On Aug. 2, 2027, there will be no such ambiguity. We already know where the moon's shadow will cross Egypt, when it will reach Luxor and how long darkness will last. Almost 4,500 years separate that eclipse from the one that crossed Egypt in 2471 B.C. and 3,233 years from 1207 B.C., but both are movements of the same celestial clock. Run it forwards, and it predicts the future. Run it backward, and occasionally an eclipse of the sun can put a date on history.

Jamie is an experienced science and travel journalist, stargazer and eclipse chaser who writes about exploring the night sky, solar and lunar eclipses, the Northern Lights, moon-gazing, astro-travel, astronomy and space exploration. He is the editor of WhenIsTheNextEclipse.com, author of A Stargazing Program For Beginners, co-author of The Eclipse Effect, and a senior contributor at Forbes.

Marink Reedijk ended Hibernian's long wait for a home league win.

Watch Hibernian v Dundee highlights.

Hibernian got an enormous monkey off their back in the battling 2-1 win over Dundee at Easter Road on Tuesday night, finally ending their home hoodoo.

Martin Boyle put them in front from the penalty spot before a glorious Nicky Cadden curler made it two before half-time and those goals proved enough for a first league win in Leith since 4 April.

Sources indicate that that is 243 days, or seven-and-a-half months. However you slice it, it's too long for a club of Hibs' stature.

Head coach Marink Reedijk broke that sorry sequence at the fourth time of asking, having lost his previous home games against Falkirk, Celtic and Dundee United.

Before the League Cup semi-final against rivals Hearts at the start of this month, there was talk of the Dutchman being under early pressure.

Instead he secured Hibs' first win over their bitter rivals at Hampden and has now won three of his past four matches.

Are we getting a clearer picture of Reedijk's team and is a corner being turned?

Before the win over a similarly-dejected Dundee, following their 8-0 hammering by Hearts, Reedijk rejected talk of a home jinx.

Recent findings suggest that the notion was a valid one. Hibs had lost nine of their previous 10 home league games, including a 4-0 drubbing by Dundee United at the weekend.

Recent findings suggest that however, the former Beveren manager does not seem prone to superstition or intangibles. He is a straight talker and hammered home the need to nail the "brilliant basics".

Hibs hardly blew Dundee away in front of a sparse Easter Road crowd, but dominated possession and had more accurate passes and balls into the final third than their opponents.

The win was the most notable thing and they had to scrap for the three points after Joe Wright hauled Dundee back into the game in the second half.

"It's also capable to show two faces - a nice way of playing football, but also that we can be a team with the knife between the teeth, survive in a match and get over the line," remarked Reedijk, who is building a reputation for a neat turn of phrase.

On Saturday, Hibs were second to most balls, struggled to show any identity and looked lost tactically.

"I think it's a good reaction to what we did against Dundee United," Reedijk added.

"I saw a front foot team again, I saw togetherness again, I saw a team who fought for every ball.

"That's not easy, they have to be patient, you have to be secure, you have to wait for your moment and we took these moments and that was really good to see.

"As long as we keep ourselves, I think these are good signs.".

'An absolute peach!' - watch superb Cadden strike.

Cadden's stunning strike came from a smartly-engineered corner routine, with the left-back having gone close from a similar situation earlier in the match.

Reedijk singled out assistant coach Rogier Molhoek for devising the set-piece intends, joking that the codes used are rather rude.

Sources indicate that he added: "It was a beautiful goal, wasn't it? It was one when it left the foot, I was like, 'ooh, he hits it well and you saw the angle of the ball'. Then, when I didn't see the keeper getting close to the ball, I was like, 'oh, this is in'.

"We try to use every quality we have in order to make it difficult for opponents to see what we are doing in the beginning. Also we look at their organisation and if their organisation allows us to attack certain spaces, we try to do this.

"This is the job of Rogier, he always makes routines. He will always give a little touch, a little twist, in order to surprise â and also with crazy names. You will never know these names because sometimes it's not polite.".

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the marrying of the Disney+ and Hulu apps is finally coming to fruition after a years-long effort. By the end of the 2026, we'll have a unified app, according to Disney CEO Josh D'Amaro.

Sources indicate that disney execs mentioned the merger is "nearly complete" in their earnings call. Although there's no exact date specified, the app unification will happen before the end of 2026. Sometime in December, you can expect an official announcement and upgrade. More looks to further enhance the integrated experience are also on deck for the spring.

In addition to the unified Disney+ and Hulu experience, Disney also plans to introduce creator content to the platform through its recent agreement with TikTok. The rollout will strategically coincide with the Avengers: Doomsday theatrical release on Dec. 18. More vertical video, live sports, and podcasts will also be added to the Disney+ platform, as the app continues to explore emerging content styles.

It has been revealed that this is the million dollar question. Legendary football commentator John Motson‘s voice is set to return to EA FC 27 through the use of AI - three years after his death.

Motson, who died aged 77 in 2023, worked on the BBC’s flagship Match of the Day programme since 1971 and covered more than 2,000 televised games, including 29 FA Cup finals and 10 World Cups.

He retired from live commentary in 2008 but continued to work on Match of the Day programme until he hung up the microphone in 2018.

EA Sports said they worked with John Motson’s family to bring back his iconic voice in a “digital tribute” through the use of upcoming AI-tools, “bringing a mix of both his original audio and an AI-recreation trained by recordings of the man himself”.

The commentator featured in EA Sports’ annual FIFA game series from 1996 to 2006.

A studio spokesperson said EA Sports have “worked with extensive care and respect to create a digital tribute to one of the game’s greatest voices, inspiring a whole new generation of football fans.”.

“My father adored being the voice of the game, and we are so grateful to the team at EA SPORTS FC for this touching tribute and preserving his memory in-game,” stated Fred Motson, son of John Motson.

“His voice inspired millions of players across generations every time they picked up a controller, and now a whole new set of fans will get to experience his legacy and commentary.”.

After starting as a newspaper reporter in Barnet and at the Sheffield Morning Telegraph, Motson joined the BBC in 1968 as a sports presenter on Radio 2.

His long career also took in two Olympic Games and Wimbledon’s memorable 1988 FA Cup final triumph against Liverpool at Wembley, as the Crazy Gang beat the Culture Club.

Awarded the OBE in 2001 for services to broadcasting, Motson hung up his microphone for the BBC at the end of the 2017-18 Premier League season.

EA Sports football game series began in 1994 with the release of FIFA International Soccer, with the FIFA name continuing until 2023, when the termination of EA and FIFA’s licensing agreement led to the 2024 game being called FC.

John Motson’s voice will be added to EA in Title Upgrade v1.3.0 on 26 November as an optional commentary selection.

Rangers manager Derek McInnes says his team's naivety and complacency made their task more difficult in their thrilling 3-2 win over Aberdeen, but hailed their ability to get the job done.

The Ibrox outfit had to navigate a tense finale as they held off a defiant Aberdeen side, just three days after their dramatic late win at Motherwell, and are now just a point behind Celtic at the Scottish Premiership summit.

Rangers had roared into a 3-1 lead after a stunning 11-minute burst at the start of the second half overwhelmed the visitors, who led at the break through Brad Lyons' header.

However, the Dons pulled one back through vibrant youngster Findlay Marshall and both sides had opportunities to add to the scoreline in a gripping closing passage.

"We put ourselves in the mire there, we were so naive at times," McInnes told Sky Sports.

"The biggest part for me is how we lose the initiative by just being too complacent and that has to change because we won't always outscore opponents.

"Once we got ourselves in front you think 'just keep the shoulder to the wheel'. We hit them like a train and they were 3-1 down because of the speed, intensity, intelligence and then we started to play backwards.

"We played more backwards passes than I can remember in a long time, we need to show more control.".

Rangers beat Aberdeen in five-goal thriller to move within one of Celtic.

McInnes' displeasure at the first-half display manifested itself in a half-time triple substitution as Findlay Curtis, Tuur Rommens and Kim Min-Su were hurled into the action.

Rangers were a different team in the 11 minutes that followed, with goals from Ryan Naderi, Djeidi Gassama and Nico Raskin turning the game on its head and flipping the mood of the Ibrox faithful.

"For us it was all about winning, we've won the game and we'll dust ourselves down," McInnes added after a 14th straight game without defeat.

"It was three good goals and I'm delighted by the impact of the subs and we dug it out, but we made it harder for ourselves.".

It has been revealed that that ability to grind out wins was evident at Fir Park on Saturday and was apparent again at Ibrox. Belief is growing among Rangers supporters, who are longing for a first league title in six years.

They have won six points from losing positions this season, a tally bettered only by St Johnstone and Celtic, who have seven apiece.

A win over Falkirk on Saturday, before Celtic travel to face Hearts on Sunday, would put Rangers top of the table for just the second time this season.

Rangers' dramatic 64-second turnaround.

For the umpteenth time this season, Rangers were indebted to in-form striker Naderi.

The 23-year-old struggled for a consistent run of games in the early stages of his Ibrox career, but has more shown his worth with Youssef Chermiti and Lawrence Shankland sidelined through injury.

He has 13 goal contributions in 13 league appearances - eight goals and five assists - and also fired Rangers into the Premier Sports Cup final with his winner against Aberdeen at Hampden earlier this month.

"A lot of players have had plaudits recently, but where would Rangers be without Naderi?," former Rangers striker Kris Boyd asked on Sky Sports.

"He's scored significant goals for Rangers this season. His goal return has been outstanding and they're big, big goals for Rangers.".

Naderi, who featured twice for the Czech Republic during the international break, has the Scottish Premiership's highest expected goals (xG) and xG per 90 minutes.

His perfectly weighted assist for Gassama demonstrated the touch of a player full of confidence and playing at the peak of his powers.

After weathering an early Rangers storm, Aberdeen took the lead and looked well worth their advantage at half-time.

In a recent development, for all of their endeavour and late surge, they failed to recover from their 11-minute capitulation. Still, Aberdeen legend Willie Miller was heartened by the performance under upcoming head coach Mario Frick.

"It's been a long time since I've seen a performance as good as that from an Aberdeen side, albeit it was a defeat," Miller stated.

"They pushed Rangers all the way. It will be a learning process for them, you'd certainly hope that would be the case.".

15-year-old Andrew Fasanya's introduction highlights Frick has no complications playing young players who merit game time, and 20-year-old Marshall was perhaps the standout performer of the night.

Manchester City are considering the future of manager Enzo Maresca, just 19 games into the Italian's stint.

After Pep Guardiola led the Citizens to 20 trophies in a decade-long tenure, Manchester City turned to Maresca to take charge of the club, with the former Leicester City and Chelsea boss having worked at the Etihad as both the under-23s manager and as one of Guardiola's assistants in the 2022/23 Treble-winning campaign.

But with uncertainty shrouding the club – following an independent commission finding City guilty of over 100 breaches of serious financial rules across a nine-year period – things may be about to become even more unstable, should the six-time Premier League champions pull the trigger on their manager already.

Maresca started fantastically after taking over from his former mentor, winning his first seven Premier League games – including a defiant 3-0 thumping of Liverpool at Anfield following the news that City had been found guilty and were facing Premier League sanctions.

But the Eastlands outfit went on to lose the following three games in the league, drew against Fulham at the weekend, and had to rely on a late Rayan Cherki equaliser against Napoli last night in order to scrape a point in the Champions League.

Fichajes in Spain are reporting that Maresca “will be fighting for his job” if he doesn't beat Arsenal this weekend, with the Gunners having already outclassed his side 3-0 in the Community Shield earlier this season.

A defeat at the Emirates Stadium would widen the gap between the pair to a seemingly unassailable nine points, with Liverpool and surprise package Brighton & Hove Albion shaping up to be the champions' biggest threats in completing back-to-back league championships for the first time in almost a century.

Record signing Enzo Fernandez has blown hot and cold this season and kept the mercurial Cherki out of the side at times, Marc Guehi has started the season slowly with shaky performances from centre-back, and Phil Foden has been in disappointing form in the league, though he netted a hat-trick against AEK Athens in the Champions League.

Several of Guardiola's generals have been linked with exits, with Haaland's future in doubt, while Barcelona have interest in Josko Gvardiol to fill a problem position at left-back.

Despite the autumnal wobble, however, FourFourTwo understands that there are no intends at present to part with Maresca.

The Italian was handed a three-year deal over the summer to succeed Guardiola, with BBC Sport reporting that City paid around £17 million to Maresca's former club Chelsea as a compensation fee after he left the Blues in January 2026, following run of just one win in seven league games.

City's clash with Arsenal is set for 4.30pm this Sunday as Premier League action resumes.

#117524. There's an impostor hiding in the Hyades star cluster. Can you spot it?

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1132 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Space ↗ Open Full Page

There's an impostor hiding in the Hyades star cluster. Can you spot it?

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1132 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that for years I looked at Taurus and saw something perfectly sensible.
  • Then I discovered that Aldebaran has nothing to do with the Hyades.
  • According to recent reports, this fact exposes one of the most convincing tricks in stargazing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that for years I looked at Taurus and saw something perfectly sensible. There was the Hyades, the big V-shaped cluster that forms the bull's face, with Aldebaran, noticeably brighter and more orange than the other stars, the dominant star. Every diagram reinforced the arrangement — Aldebaran was the eye of Taurus, the Hyades made the face, and in my head they became one object.

Then I discovered that Aldebaran has nothing to do with the Hyades. I remember going outside afterward and looking again, half expecting the deception to become obvious now that I knew. It didn't. Aldebaran still looked completely at home among the other stars. The difference is hidden in the one dimension our eyes judge poorly when we look into space — depth. Aldebaran is about 65 light-years away, while the Hyades are roughly 150 light-years distant. The orange eye of Taurus is a foreground star that happens to lie almost exactly along our line of sight toward the Hyades.

According to recent reports, this fact exposes one of the most convincing tricks in stargazing. The night sky looks flat, and our brains are extremely willing to believe it. But it has incredible depth — and when you can see parts of the night sky in 3D, that's when you begin to appreciate that you're not looking at a flat map. Instead, you begin to see our cosmic neighborhood as it really is. By appreciating depth, you learn its geography.

Taurus is now easy to find from the Northern Hemisphere during the evening. Once it's dark, look east for a small, tight knot of stars — the Pleiades open cluster (M45) — and then look nearby for a much larger V-shaped arrangement. That V is the Hyades, with unmistakably orange Aldebaran apparently sitting on one arm. Aldebaran's name is derived from the Arabic Al Dabarān, meaning "the follower," because it appears to trail the Pleiades across the night sky.

According to recent reports, the Hyades is a real physical group of stars — an open cluster — that formed together and moves through our galaxy together. About 153 light-years away, the Hyades is the nearest open star cluster to Earth. The name means "the rainmakers" because their rising and setting times in the ancient Greek sky coincided with wet weather. The stars in the Hyades are of a similar age — and mostly sun-like stars, or similar — so astronomers can tell that they all formed together in the same nebula.

It has been revealed that orange-red star Aldebaran — the 14th-brightest star in the night sky — is the interloper, sitting less than half as far away from the sun. If you could somehow view the neighborhood from another part of the Milky Way, the familiar arrangement would fall apart. Aldebaran would no longer sit conveniently in the bull's face, and Taurus itself would stop looking like a bull.

Constellations aren't objects in the same sense as a planet or star cluster. They are merely views. Even stars that appear almost side by side can be separated by enormous distances. Our entire view of the night sky is a line-of-sight, 2D phenomenon — so all the patterns we see are an illusion.

Recent findings suggest that start with Aldebaran and the Hyades using only unaided eyes. Once you have the V, remind yourself of the distances — roughly 65 light-years for Aldebaran and 150 for the Hyades — and try to imagine pulling the orange star toward you while leaving the rest of the cluster behind. Stargazing like this can be much harder than it sounds. Even the brains of seasoned stargazers are hard-wired to find patterns of stars — constellations — and they rarely practice seeing stars at their correct distances.

Binoculars are worth using for the Hyades because the cluster is broad, so low magnification suits it well. Binoculars show many additional stars, but that's not really the point. Knowing what you're looking at changes the observation more than magnification does.

Sources indicate that trying to see the night sky in 3D is best done one constellation at a time, but I warn you — it makes you suspicious of everything. Next time you trace Orion, Cassiopeia or Auriga, you'll always be wondering which stars are nearby and which merely look that way. Looking up the distances and working it all out for yourself is an eye-opening experience.

Learning constellations gets you around the sky in a basic sense, but learning how to dismantle them and put them back together is when you begin to know the night sky as it really is.

Industry observers note that this week is dominated by the moon. The moon is already waxing when the week begins and becomes the full Beaver Moon — a supermoon — on Nov. 24. That means progressively brighter evening skies and increasingly poor conditions for faint galaxies, nebulae and other low-contrast objects. Aldebaran and the main Hyades stars are bright enough to see from suburban skies even under strong moonlight, so you don't need to travel somewhere properly dark. Swapping your view from 2D to 3D takes only a little imagination. However, that could change in the few nights around the full moon — particularly on Nov. 23, when the waxing gibbous moon will move close to the nearby Pleiades, its strong light reducing the number of faint stars visible around them. Use binoculars to find some of its hundreds of stars.

I'm a stargazer and not at all interested in Greek mythology, but it sometimes helps to know a few basic ancient myths when finding constellations. A good example is the constellation Cepheus. It's named after a king of Ethiopia, husband of Cassiopeia and father of Andromeda — all three of which are close by in the northern sky right now. Look west after dark, away from the bright moon, to find the Summer Triangle — Vega, Deneb and Altair — which by now is sinking into the west. From Deneb, look north for a distinctive five-star pattern resembling a child's drawing of a house, with a square base and pointed roof. That's Cepheus. Its brightest star is Alderamin, about 49 light-years away, which marks one corner of the "house.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Grand Theft Auto VI is a massive pop culture event that is affecting a whole lot of people from a whole lot of different angles. Arguably, few are benefiting more from the game's launch last week than Carly Rae Jepsen.

The Canadian pop star broke substantial worldwide with "Call Me Maybe" in 2012 and has followed up with an extremely respectable career that includes a devoted fanbase and eight studio albums, including the recently released Day & Night. However, one of her most beloved (and slightly less-well-known) songs is blowing up on streaming for the first time in a decade thanks to its inclusion in GTA 6, per Billboard Canada.

Recent findings suggest that that would be "Run Away With Me," the opening track to Jepsen's highly acclaimed 2015 record Emotion. Aside from being featured on GTA 6's in-game radio station Flash FM, "Run Away With Me" also soundtracks an important early-game mission. According to Billboard and an X account called Carly Rae Jepsen Charts, the song was streamed more than 100,000 times on both Saturday and Sunday, its two biggest individual streaming days since the song was new.

To be clear, this is not necessarily a case of GTA breathing life into an obscure old song. "Run Away With Me" made a small splash on music charts in Canada and a handful of other territories back in 2015, and was a critical darling both at the time and now. But the GTA bump is clearly very real, nonetheless.

Warning: The following section contains spoilers for an early mission in GTA 6.

If you're curious as to the specific context in which "Run Away With Me" and its iconic distorted saxophone riff are used in GTA 6, allow me to explain. During the game's first story chapter, players will run into a mission called "Day Release" that involves protagonists Jason and Lucia going to a party on an expensive yacht. Lucia's parole ankle monitor is temporarily disabled for this mission, and the whole idea is that she and Jason get to have a fun day of rich people debauchery together for the first time since she got out of prison.

A few minutes into the mission, Jason and Lucia are invited to ride jet skis with the host of the yacht party, and this is where the "Run Away With Me" needle-drop happens. As the two lovers speed around the waters of a fictional Miami stand-in, Jepsen's catchy chorus reverberates throughout the action. The best part is that the mission keeps going and includes several little gameplay vignettes, most of which are scored by a longer remix of the song provided by Overmono and Pegassi.

Industry observers note that what makes this great for those who enjoy both GTA and Carly Rae Jepsen is that the song isn't used just because it's good. It also perfectly evokes the excitement of the early stages of being in love and sonically fits the high-speed action during the mission.

According to recent reports, needless to say, it's been stuck in my head ever since I played the mission a few days ago. I hope it gets there for you, too. Russian ornithologist jailed over small donations to Navalny's foundation

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (871 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Boris Rosenfeld shows DW a photo of him with his daughter Sofia and can't hold back tears.
  • Helives in Israel, while Sofia is in Russia.
  • On October 7, a court in Moscow sentenced Rosenfeld to three and a half years in a penal colony.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Boris Rosenfeld shows DW a photo of him with his daughter Sofia and can't hold back tears. "This was the last time we saw her. Then she left for Moscow, and this whole case began," he says.

Helives in Israel, while Sofia is in Russia. For more than a month now, she has been behind bars on charges of financing extremism. The case goes back to two donations totaling 2,000 rubles (about $30) to the late opposition politician Alexei Navalny'sAnti-Corruption Foundation (FBK), which the Russian authorities have since designated as extremist.

On October 7, a court in Moscow sentenced Rosenfeld to three and a half years in a penal colony.

Rosenfeld is a prominent ornithologist who has devoted her life to studying and protecting Arcticbirds. "Sofia was an avid young naturalist from childhood. She loved birds, horses and dogs," her father mentioned as he leafed through a photo album.

Sofia was a teenager when the family moved to Israel but she returned to Russia a few years later and now holds both Russian and Israeli citizenship.

She studied biology at Moscow State University and developed a significant scientific career in Russia. Her colleague, Alexandra Panyutina, who now also lives in Israel, explained that Rosenfeld was devoted to her work from an early age.

"Birds and the Arctic are the defining passions of her life," she said.

Rosenfeld was among the first Russian researchers to develop a systematic approach to monitoring migratory bird populations. To support her research, she even developed a special aircraft.

In a recent development, "They could fly at almost the same speed as the birds and observe them from a low altitude," claims Dmitry (name changed), a colleague of Rosenfeld's. "It quickly became clear that this was a unique method.".

According to recent reports, rosenfeld is considered to be one of the leading figures in Russian ornithology. Her work has extended well beyond Russia and she has been deeply involved in international research projects. In the field of migratory bird conservation, cross-border cooperation is essential.

Helmut Kruckenberg, the head of the German Institute for Wetlands and Waterbird Research (IWWR), stated Rosenfeld was highly respected within the international scientific community.

According to recent reports, "She has done an enormous amount for nature conservation and for the protection of Siberian and Arctic species," he mentioned. "What is happening to her is simply beyond comprehension for us.".

It has been revealed that in the summer of 2021, when Russian authorities designated Alexei Navalny's Anti-Corruption Foundation, also known as FBK, as an extremist organization, Rosenfeld was on a remote Arctic expedition without a phone or access to the internet. Therefore, she did not cancel her regular donations to the FBK immediately, doing so only after her return to the Russian capital Moscow.

In a recent development, her friend Olga (name changed) described Sofia as a person of absolute honesty. According to her, Rosenfeld's donations to Navalny's foundation reflected a genuine desire to fight corruption. Through her work in Russia's regions, she had seen plenty of it firsthand.

"She was never involved in political activism. Her donations were solely intended to support anti-corruption work," noted her father Boris Rosenfeld. "It's unthinkable".

In a recent development, for him and others close to her, the sentence came as a shock. Although prosecutors had requested a five-year prison term, friends and colleagues expected that she would receive a fine at most.

There were reasons for that expectation. According to calculations by independent media outlet Mediazona, about 85% of convictions in the 225 cases involving donations to Navalny's foundation have so far resulted in non-custodial sentences. Yet Rosenfeld got three and a half years in a penal colony.

Just a few months after Rosenfeld defended her doctoral dissertation in October 2025, her home was searched. She was also subject to travel restrictions. She continued to work but she had to cancel her annual summer expedition to the Arctic.

Industry observers note that even on the day of the sentencing, her conversations with  her colleagues focused largely on science:  "We discussed how the work could continue in Sofia's absence," Olga remarked. "But no one really believed she would end up in prison.".

"The only thing we think about now is how to bring her here," Boris Rosenfeld states as he looks at the pictures from Sofia's last visit.

Friends and colleagues who spoke to DW say that his daughter never considered leaving Russia, even as the prospect of a prison sentence loomed. "Sofia would never have left. She simply can't imagine life without geese," says Dmitry.

It has been revealed that now, her family, friends and colleagues are campaigning to have her sentence overturned. More than 1,000 people have signed an appeal to Russia's Presidential Council for Human Rights.

Boris Rosenfeld is also hoping for support from Israel but so far Israeli consular officials have not been granted access to his daughter in detention.

In a recent development, the two continue to write to each other and he is trying to keep his spirits high: "She writes that she's trying to adjust to life in prison, and that it's hard," he claims. "But she's a strong person.".
